title: Historical-to-future pattern-effect correction
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: How will geographical patterns of ocean warming shape the planet's radiative feedback over the coming century — and can we deduce long-term climate sensitivity from the historical record alone, without having to guess the uncertain future sea-surface-temperature pattern? A successful theory would map historical pattern effects into a correction for future feedbacks.
status: Intensive work since the 2010s demonstrates substantial historical effective-sensitivity biases in model experiments; the real-world correction remains uncertain. Key work: Gregory et al. (2020; online 2019), ["How accurately can the climate sensitivity to CO₂ be estimated from historical climate change?"](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-019-04991-y).
solved_when: A method exists that infers long-term (equilibrium) climate sensitivity from historical observations without prescribing the future sea-surface-temperature pattern, and that predicts how shifting geographical warming patterns alter global radiative feedback.
why: It is the missing link between how fast the planet has warmed so far and how fast it will warm in the future; without it, historical observations cannot be trusted as a guide to future climate sensitivity.
key_works: Gregory et al. (2020; online 2019), [“How accurately can the climate sensitivity to CO₂ be estimated from historical climate change?”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-019-04991-y).

title: Transferable trade-cumulus feedback constraints
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Does the trade-cumulus cloud feedback remain weak as conditions change — across seasons, ocean basins, mesoscale cloud organizations, and warmer climates? More formally, which observed relationships between clouds and circulation are robust enough to transfer to environments other than those in which they were measured?
status: EUREC4A observations reported in 2022 (Vogel et al., "Strong cloud–circulation coupling explains weak trade cumulus feedback") refuted a strong mixing-desiccation feedback in the sampled conditions and supported a weak feedback; whether these findings transfer more broadly remains open.
solved_when: A quantitative characterization of the trade-cumulus feedback is established that holds across seasons, basins, mesoscale organizations, and warmer climates, identifying which cloud–circulation relationships transfer under shifting environmental conditions.
why: Trade-cumulus mixing-desiccation is an influential mechanism driving high climate sensitivity in models; confirming or constraining its strength directly tests whether such high-sensitivity projections are credible.
key_works: Vogel et al. (2022), [“Strong cloud–circulation coupling explains weak trade cumulus feedback”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05364-y).

title: Tropical anvil optical-depth feedback
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: How do tropical anvil clouds change their optical properties as the climate warms — specifically their ice mass, particle sizes, optical depth, and life cycles — and what shortwave-plus-longwave feedback does this produce, independent of any change in anvil cloud area?
status: McKim, Bony and Dufresne (2024), ["Weak anvil cloud area feedback suggested by physical and observational constraints"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-024-01414-4), substantially constrained the area contribution in 2024 while identifying anvil albedo feedback as unresolved.
solved_when: The warming-induced changes in tropical-anvil ice mass, particle sizes, optical depth, and life cycles are determined, and the resulting combined shortwave-plus-longwave (anvil albedo) feedback is quantified separately from the anvil-area feedback.
why: It isolates a distinct cloud-feedback component that directly affects projections of climate sensitivity; without it, the anvil contribution to warming projections remains unbounded.
key_works: McKim, Bony and Dufresne (2024), [“Weak anvil cloud area feedback suggested by physical and observational constraints”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-024-01414-4).

title: Attribution of the recent planetary-albedo decline
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: What has caused the recent decline in the sunlight Earth reflects back to space — human-driven aerosol changes, internal ocean variability, or temperature-driven cloud feedback? A complete attribution would quantitatively decompose the albedo decline among these drivers and test the decomposition against observed spectral radiation, cloud properties, ocean-temperature patterns, and heat uptake.
status: Goessling, Rackow and Jung (2025; online 2024), ["Recent global temperature surge intensified by record-low planetary albedo"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adq7280), linked the 2023 temperature surge to exceptionally low albedo, especially reduced low-cloud cover; the causes of the cloud changes remain unresolved.
solved_when: The declining reflected-sunlight signal is attributed among aerosol changes, internal ocean variability, and temperature-driven cloud feedback, in a way that is consistent with spectral radiation measurements, cloud-property observations, ocean-temperature patterns, and heat uptake.
why: It determines whether the albedo decline reflects a persistent cloud feedback or forcing change, or merely transient variability — with direct consequences for how much additional warming we should expect.
key_works: Goessling, Rackow and Jung (2025; online 2024), [“Recent global temperature surge intensified by record-low planetary albedo”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adq7280).

title: Convective self-aggregation in the real tropical atmosphere
open: When does the spontaneous clustering of convection seen in idealized simulations actually govern how storms organize in the real tropical atmosphere? More precisely, can we predict how aggregation depends on temperature, rotation, domain size, wind shear, and surface coupling?
status: The phenomenon has been studied since the 1990s; the RCEMIP intercomparison (Wing et al., 2020, ["Clouds and Convective Self-Aggregation in a Multimodel Ensemble of Radiative-Convective Equilibrium Simulations"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020MS002138)) reproduced aggregation across many models in 2020 but exposed substantial disagreement under standardized conditions.
solved_when: A predictive theory or framework exists that links idealized radiative-convective equilibrium aggregation to observed tropical organization and correctly predicts its dependence on temperature, rotation, domain size, shear, and surface coupling.
why: It would connect mesoscale storm behavior to humidity, radiation, and precipitation extremes, anchoring a key link between small-scale convection and large-scale tropical climate.
key_works: Wing et al. (2020), [“Clouds and Convective Self-Aggregation in a Multimodel Ensemble of Radiative-Convective Equilibrium Simulations”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020MS002138).

title: Scale-aware entrainment and detrainment closure
open: Can we derive a single set of entrainment and detrainment laws governing the exchange between clouds and their environment that remains valid from shallow cumulus through deep convection, and across changes in model resolution? Formally, the goal is a closure predicting dilution and mass-flux profiles without regime-specific retuning.
status: A decades-old problem. Large-eddy simulations constrain individual cases, but organized exchange and turbulent mixing remain difficult to generalize. Key works: de Rooy et al. (2013), ["Entrainment and detrainment in cumulus convection: an overview"](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.1959).
solved_when: A scale-aware closure is derived that predicts dilution and mass-flux profiles across the full range from shallow cumulus to deep convection as resolution varies, with no regime-specific retuning.
why: A solution would improve rainfall, cloud feedback, and tropical circulation together — a joint constraint these phenomena currently lack.
key_works: de Rooy et al. (2013), [“Entrainment and detrainment in cumulus convection: an overview”](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.1959).

title: A discriminating theory of the Madden–Julian oscillation
open: What physical mechanisms govern the Madden–Julian oscillation — its initiation, eastward propagation, horizontal scale, and termination, including its passage across the Maritime Continent? A satisfying theory must not only reproduce these features but yield observables that discriminate among the competing moisture, wave, and ocean-coupling explanations.
status: Open since the oscillation's discovery in 1971–1972. Existing theories reproduce important features of the MJO, but the 2020 fifty-year assessment (Jiang et al. 2020, "Fifty Years of Research on the Madden-Julian Oscillation: Recent Progress, Challenges, and Perspectives," https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JD030911) found major questions about mechanism and prediction still unresolved.
solved_when: A mechanism (or set of mechanisms) is identified that explains MJO initiation, eastward propagation, scale, and termination, and from which observations can be derived that distinguish the competing moisture, wave, and ocean-coupling theories, including behavior during Maritime Continent passage.
why: Resolving it extends useful prediction of tropical rainfall and of remote weather extremes driven by the MJO.
key_works: Jiang et al. (2020), [“Fifty Years of Research on the Madden-Julian Oscillation: Recent Progress, Challenges, and Perspectives”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JD030911).

title: Forced changes in ENSO diversity and amplitude
open: How does anthropogenic warming reshape ENSO's diversity and strength — shifting the balance between eastern-Pacific and central-Pacific El Niño events, La Niña persistence, amplitude, and event-to-event transition probabilities? A formal answer would provide quantified estimates of these changes that can be cleanly separated from the backdrop of internal multidecadal variability.
status: After decades of research, Cai et al. (2021) synthesized increasing evidence that selected models project stronger variability, but quantitative projections remain uncertain.
solved_when: Warming-driven changes in eastern- versus central-Pacific El Niño occurrence, La Niña persistence, amplitude, and transition probabilities are quantified, and the forced signal is distinguished from multidecadal variability with stated uncertainty.
why: These ENSO characteristics govern the connected drought, flood, ecosystem, and agricultural hazards that societies plan around, so knowing how they shift determines future hazard exposure.
key_works: Cai et al. (2021), [“Changing El Niño–Southern Oscillation in a warming climate”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-021-00199-z).

title: Tropical Pacific observed–modeled trend discrepancy
open: Why have equatorial Pacific temperature-gradient trends over recent decades diverged between observations and coupled model simulations? A satisfying answer must disentangle the contributions of internal variability, model dynamical biases, aerosol forcing, and errors in the observational record itself.
status: The discrepancy has persisted across model generations; Seager, Henderson and Cane (2022) documented discrepancies extending beyond individual ENSO events ([“Persistent Discrepancies between Observed and Modeled Trends in the Tropical Pacific Ocean”](https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-21-0648.1)).
solved_when: A quantitatively attributed account of the observed–modeled multidecadal trend discrepancy exists, assigning weights to internal variability, dynamical biases, aerosol forcing, and observational errors sufficient to reconcile the observed and modeled equatorial Pacific gradient trends.
why: The spatial pattern of Pacific warming governs global climate feedback strength and regional drought risk, so unexplained trend discrepancies undermine confidence in projections of both.
key_works: Seager, Henderson and Cane (2022), [“Persistent Discrepancies between Observed and Modeled Trends in the Tropical Pacific Ocean”](https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-21-0648.1).

title: The climate signal-to-noise paradox
open: Why do some initialized climate ensembles predict real-world observations better than they predict their own members — exceeding the skill their apparently weak predictable signal should allow? A full explanation should identify the mechanism (e.g., too-weak signal response, excessive noise, sampling error, or ensemble construction) and provide a correction that restores consistency.
status: The paradox has been prominent since 2014 and was formalized by Scaife and Smith (2018), "A signal-to-noise paradox in climate science" (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-018-0038-4). A 2024 community reassessment, Weisheimer et al. (2024), "The Signal-to-Noise Paradox in Climate Forecasts: Revisiting Our Understanding and Identifying Future Priorities" (https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0019.1), found no conclusive general resolution.
solved_when: A validated account of the paradox that identifies which cause — weak responses, excessive noise, sampling, or ensemble-construction effects — operates, together with a correction that removes the inconsistency between apparent signal and achieved forecast skill, confirmed as a general resolution.
why: Resolving it would unlock additional seasonal and decadal forecast skill beyond what current ensembles deliver.
key_works: Scaife and Smith (2018), [“A signal-to-noise paradox in climate science”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-018-0038-4); Weisheimer et al. (2024), [“The Signal-to-Noise Paradox in Climate Forecasts: Revisiting Our Understanding and Identifying Future Priorities”](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0019.1).

title: Global closure of boundary-driven abyssal upwelling
open: How much of the ocean's deep-water upwelling takes place in the thin turbulent boundary layers that hug sloping seafloors, rather than in the interior? More precisely, can local measurements of boundary-layer upwelling be scaled up to basin-wide transports in a way that closes the abyssal energy budget?
status: A 2024 dye experiment (Wynne-Cattanach et al. (2024), "Observations of diapycnal upwelling within a sloping submarine canyon," https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07411-2) directly observed strong diapycnal upwelling in one submarine canyon; whether such upwelling is globally prevalent, and how to parameterize it, remains open.
solved_when: A quantitative closure exists that scales local boundary-layer observations to basin-scale overturning transports while satisfying the global energy budget.
why: It would link small-scale turbulent mixing to the global overturning circulation, turning canyon-scale dye measurements into usable physics for climate-scale ocean models.
key_works: Wynne-Cattanach et al. (2024), [“Observations of diapycnal upwelling within a sloping submarine canyon”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07411-2).

title: Conditions for self-sustaining marine ice-cliff failure
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Under what conditions can marine ice-cliff failure become self-sustaining, so that retreat accelerates faster than viscous thinning, mélange buttressing, and geometric stabilization can arrest it? The goal is a set of observationally constrained criteria distinguishing sustained cliff-driven retreat from episodic, self-limiting failure.
status: The question has been influential since the 2010s. Morlighem et al. (2024) found that stabilizing processes can prevent MICI in modeled twenty-first-century settings ["The West Antarctic Ice Sheet may not be vulnerable to marine ice cliff instability during the 21st century"](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ado7794).
solved_when: Observationally constrained conditions are established that specify when cliff failure outruns the stabilizing processes of viscous thinning, mélange buttressing, and geometric stabilization — or, conversely, when those processes necessarily prevent self-sustaining retreat.
why: It tests whether marine ice cliff instability (MICI) is a real contributor to high-end sea-level projections or an artifact of unconstrained model assumptions.
key_works: Morlighem et al. (2024), [“The West Antarctic Ice Sheet may not be vulnerable to marine ice cliff instability during the 21st century”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ado7794).

title: Three-dimensional solid-Earth feedback on Antarctic retreat
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Can mantle viscosity and lithospheric structure beneath Antarctica be constrained well enough that glacial-isostatic adjustment, sea-level, and ice-sheet models close the loop jointly — predicting solid-Earth unloading, uplift, gravitational change, and ocean water redistribution together with ice retreat itself?
status: Gomez et al. (2024), ["The influence of realistic 3D mantle viscosity on Antarctica's contribution to future global sea levels"](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adn1470), showed that realistic three-dimensional structure materially changes projected sea levels; that structure remains incompletely observed.
solved_when: A jointly inferred three-dimensional viscosity and lithospheric structure enables a coupled prediction of unloading, uplift, gravitational changes, water redistribution, and ice retreat that materially improves on current projections.
why: Solid-Earth rebound feeds back on both ice-sheet stability and regional sea-level fingerprints, so without it, projections of Antarctic retreat and its sea-level impact are systematically biased.
key_works: Gomez et al. (2024), [“The influence of realistic 3D mantle viscosity on Antarctica’s contribution to future global sea levels”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adn1470).

title: Persistence and reversibility of the Antarctic low-sea-ice state
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Has Antarctic sea ice undergone a persistent transition to a new low-ice state, or is the recent behavior a long-lived forced response or unusual variability? More precisely, determine whether the post-2016 decline reflects a regime shift, and identify the physical conditions under which the sea-ice system could recover its earlier state.
status: The question sharpened after 2016, when Antarctic sea ice dropped abruptly. Raphael et al. (2025) ([“A twenty-first century structural change in Antarctica’s sea ice system”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02107-5)) found a structural statistical change, which alone does not demonstrate irreversible bifurcation.
solved_when: A statistically rigorous characterization distinguishes persistent transition, forced response, and internal variability for the observed Antarctic sea-ice record, and specifies the physical conditions permitting or precluding recovery.
why: The answer governs Southern Ocean heat exchange, ecosystems, and sea-ice projections, since a persistent transition versus reversible variability implies very different futures for the region.
key_works: Raphael et al. (2025), [“A twenty-first century structural change in Antarctica’s sea ice system”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02107-5).

title: Definition-robust atmospheric-river change estimates
open: Which changes in atmospheric-river occurrence, duration, clustering, and landfall are robust to how an atmospheric river is defined? More precisely, determine which trends survive across reasonable detection definitions, and translate those definitions into physically interpretable transport and impact statistics.
status: ARTMIP compared over twenty tracking methods in 2019 and found substantial methodological dependence in atmospheric-river statistics (Rutz et al. (2019), ["The Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP): Quantifying Uncertainties in Atmospheric River Climatology"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JD030936)).
solved_when: A systematic comparison shows which occurrence, duration, clustering, and landfall change estimates are stable across reasonable detection definitions, with definitions mapped onto physically interpretable transport and impact statistics.
why: Without it, event-label choices dominate flood and water projections rather than the underlying physics.
key_works: Rutz et al. (2019), [“The Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP): Quantifying Uncertainties in Atmospheric River Climatology”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JD030936).

title: Unique causal explanation of the Mid-Pleistocene Transition
open: Why did glacial cycles shift from a predominantly 41,000-year rhythm to larger, roughly 100,000-year rhythms around the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, without any comparable change in orbital forcing? A satisfactory answer must discriminate among the candidate mechanisms — ice-sheet growth, regolith removal, ocean circulation, and atmospheric CO₂ — and identify which actually caused the historical transition.
status: Willeit et al. (2019) reproduced the transition in a model using declining CO₂ and regolith removal, establishing that these mechanisms are jointly sufficient — but not that they are the unique historical cause.
solved_when: A mechanism (or combination) is identified that both reproduces the shift from ~41,000-year to ~100,000-year glacial cycles and is uniquely supported by the historical record, ruling out the alternative ice, regolith, ocean, and CO₂ mechanisms.
why: Resolving this would validate or falsify the nonlinear ice–climate feedbacks used in long-timescale climate models, and would turn the Mid-Pleistocene Transition from a reproduced model behavior into a genuinely explained event.
key_works: Willeit et al. (2019), [“Mid-Pleistocene transition in glacial cycles explained by declining CO₂ and regolith removal”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aav7337).

title: Absolute radiometric closure of Earth’s energy imbalance
open: Can we measure Earth's outgoing and incoming radiation so accurately and continuously that changes in the planet's energy imbalance can be resolved independently of model-based inference? Formally, this means closing the error budget — calibration, sampling, and radiance-to-flux conversion — tightly enough to be checked against observed heat storage.
status: This is a decades-old metrology challenge. CLARREO established an SI-traceable approach to the measurement, while heat inventories provide complementary constraints (Wielicki et al. (2013), ["Achieving Climate Change Absolute Accuracy in Orbit"](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-12-00149.1)).
solved_when: A sustained measurement system achieves closure: calibration, sampling, and radiance-to-flux errors are reduced to the point that the radiometrically inferred energy imbalance agrees with independent heat-storage inventories.
why: It provides a direct, model-independent measure of whether planetary heat accumulation is accelerating, and anchors the observing infrastructure needed to detect drift in the climate record.
key_works: Wielicki et al. (2013), [“Achieving Climate Change Absolute Accuracy in Orbit”](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-12-00149.1).

title: Attribution of the residual land carbon sink
open: Can we decompose the residual land carbon sink into its component causes — CO₂ fertilization, nutrient deposition, climate, regrowth, and management — at regional scales? A complete attribution would identify each process's contribution and predict withheld fluxes and vegetation-versus-soil storage partitioning consistently.
status: A decades-old problem. O’Sullivan et al. (2022), in ["Process-oriented analysis of dominant sources of uncertainty in the land carbon sink"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32416-8), showed that models agreeing globally diverge in their processes and regional responses.
solved_when: The individual contributions of CO₂ fertilization, nutrient deposition, climate, regrowth, and management to regional land carbon uptake are separated, and the attribution framework predicts withheld fluxes and the vegetation-versus-soil storage split consistently.
why: It determines how much future emissions vegetation and soil will take up, which directly constrains remaining carbon budgets.
key_works: O’Sullivan et al. (2022), [“Process-oriented analysis of dominant sources of uncertainty in the land carbon sink”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32416-8).

title: Nutrient-limited CO₂ fertilization in mature forests
open: How do nitrogen and phosphorus availability constrain the conversion of elevated-CO₂ photosynthesis into persistent ecosystem carbon? The question is what whole-ecosystem allocation patterns emerge across different forest types when nutrient limitation is manipulated over multiple years.
status: Jiang et al. (2020), in ["The fate of carbon in a mature forest under carbon dioxide enrichment"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2128-9), found that additional assimilation in a mature eucalyptus forest was largely returned through respiration; whether this fate holds across other forests remains unresolved.
solved_when: Multiyear, whole-ecosystem CO₂-enrichment manipulations across contrasting forest types yield a predictive account of how nitrogen and phosphorus constrain the fate of additional assimilated carbon.
why: It resolves a major uncertainty in the size and persistence of the future land carbon sink.
key_works: Jiang et al. (2020), [“The fate of carbon in a mature forest under carbon dioxide enrichment”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2128-9).

title: Amazon forest transition thresholds under interacting stresses
open: Where, across the Amazon basin, do the combined stresses of warming, drying, deforestation, and fire cross from reversible local degradation into a persistent loss of forest — and can we identify location-dependent thresholds that separate that outcome from a self-sustaining regional transition driven by moisture recycling?
status: Flores et al. (2024), ["Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06970-0), synthesized candidate thresholds; their ranges do not constitute validated basin-scale transition forecasts.
solved_when: Validated basin-scale forecasts exist that give location-dependent thresholds for persistent forest loss under warming, drying, deforestation, and fire, and that distinguish local degradation from self-sustaining regional moisture-recycling transitions.
why: Such thresholds pinpoint where interventions can still preserve the forest's carbon storage, biodiversity, and rainfall regime before a regional transition becomes self-sustaining.
key_works: Flores et al. (2024), [“Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06970-0).

title: Independent measurement of global OH variability
open: Can we measure the global abundance of hydroxyl radical weighted by its interaction with methane, using observations that are independent of the methane data used to infer emissions? In formal terms, the goal is to separate true OH variability from uncertainties in tracer emissions and atmospheric transport.
status: This is a decades-old attribution obstacle. The 2022 analysis of 2020 by Peng et al. (2022), ["Wetland emission and atmospheric sink changes explain methane growth in 2020"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05447-w), illustrates how material sink effects can shape inferred source growth.
solved_when: An independent observational constraint on methane-weighted global OH variability exists, capable of distinguishing OH sink changes from tracer-emission and transport uncertainty in methane source inversions.
why: It would make methane emissions verification robust to changes in the atmosphere's cleansing capacity, so inferred source trends are not confounded by sink variability.
key_works: Peng et al. (2022), [“Wetland emission and atmospheric sink changes explain methane growth in 2020”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05447-w).

title: Annual methane budgets for intermittent super-emitters
open: Can we reconstruct an annual methane budget for an intermittent super-emitter from brief, irregular observations, given that its total is dominated by a few rare emission events? Formally, this requires inferring event duration distributions and detection probabilities, with calibrated uncertainty, across different operating regimes.
status: Lauvaux et al. (2022), ["Global assessment of oil and gas methane ultra-emitters"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj4351), mapped global oil-and-gas ultra-emitters, but their snapshots do not establish annual totals for intermittent sources.
solved_when: A method exists that produces annual methane totals for intermittent super-emitters from sparse snapshot observations, with established duration distributions, detection probabilities, and calibrated uncertainties spanning operating regimes.
why: It would verify whether repairs at emitting facilities actually reduce emissions over the year, in the gaps between satellite overpasses.
key_works: Lauvaux et al. (2022), [“Global assessment of oil and gas methane ultra-emitters”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj4351).

title: Whole-profile carbon additionality of reduced tillage
open: Under what real-world conditions does reduced tillage actually generate additional soil carbon across the whole profile, once changes in bulk density, erosion, crop yields, and non-CO₂ gases are properly accounted for? In other words, can we distinguish true persistent stock increases from mere redistribution of carbon within the soil column?
status: Powlson et al. (2014), ["Limited potential of no-till agriculture for climate change mitigation"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate2292), showed that many apparent benefits reflect depth redistribution; conditional prediction remains open.
solved_when: There is a validated set of conditions (or a predictive model) under which reduced tillage produces additional whole-profile carbon stocks after corrections for density, erosion, yield effects, and other greenhouse gases, with redistribution clearly separated from persistent gains.
why: It prevents overstated carbon removals in agricultural climate accounting and identifies which management practices genuinely sequester carbon.
key_works: Powlson et al. (2014), [“Limited potential of no-till agriculture for climate change mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate2292).

title: Biological nitrification inhibition across real agricultural soils
open: Can crops be bred whose roots release nitrification inhibitors that keep working across real agricultural soils — varying in type, microbiome, and fertilizer regime — without sacrificing yield? Formally, the goal is a cultivar in which biological nitrification inhibition persists through genotype–environment–microbiome interactions and delivers whole-system nitrogen savings.
status: Subbarao et al. (2021) transferred the biological nitrification inhibition trait into wheat (["Enlisting wild grass genes to combat nitrification in wheat farming: A nature-based solution"](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106595118)), but consistent whole-system performance of the trait across field conditions remains unresolved.
solved_when: A bred cultivar demonstrates consistent suppression of nitrification across diverse soils, microbiomes, and fertilizer conditions with no yield loss, alongside measured reductions in the combined losses of N₂O, nitrogen leaching, and ammonia volatilization.
why: It would give farmers a crop-encoded route to higher nitrogen-use efficiency, cutting fertilizer waste and greenhouse-gas emissions without depending on external synthetic nitrification inhibitors.
key_works: Subbarao et al. (2021), [“Enlisting wild grass genes to combat nitrification in wheat farming: A nature-based solution”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106595118).

title: DAC sorbent lifetime under real ambient contaminants
open: Can a direct air capture sorbent hold its capacity and regeneration efficiency over the years of oxygen, humidity, aerosol, and pollutant exposure it would face in real open-air operation? More formally, can we establish and validate an accelerated-aging protocol whose predictions match observed field degradation over a sorbent's service life?

title: Equilibrium climate sensitivity without shared-evidence bias
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: How sensitive is Earth's equilibrium climate to doubled CO₂ when the evidence lines used to answer are not independent? The problem asks for a constraint on equilibrium warming that correctly accounts for statistical dependencies among historical, process-based, paleoclimate, and model evidence, so that the resulting uncertainty bounds are robust to plausible alternative aerosol histories, cloud feedbacks, and prior choices.
status: Quantitative uncertainty estimates date to the 1979 Charney assessment; in 2021, IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021, Chapter 7) narrowed the likely range to 2.5–4°C. Key works: Sherwood et al. (2020), "An Assessment of Earth's Climate Sensitivity Using Multiple Lines of Evidence" (https://doi.org/10.1029/2019RG000678); Forster et al. (2021), IPCC AR6, Chapter 7 (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-7/).
solved_when: A quantified uncertainty bound on equilibrium warming from doubled CO₂ is obtained whose credible/likely interval survives plausible alternative aerosol histories, cloud feedbacks, and priors, while the evidence synthesis explicitly and correctly models dependencies among the historical, process, paleoclimate, and model lines of evidence.
why: The answer determines which emissions and concentration pathways are compatible with given temperature targets; if the uncertainty is understated because of double-counted shared evidence, mitigation budgets derived from it are wrong.
key_works: Sherwood et al. (2020), [“An Assessment of Earth’s Climate Sensitivity Using Multiple Lines of Evidence”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019RG000678); Forster et al. (2021), [IPCC AR6, Chapter 7](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-7/).

why: It governs polar and extratropical cloud feedbacks and thus how sensitive the climate system is to warming in current models.

title: Identifiable forced and internal Atlantic multidecadal variability
open: Can we decompose observed Atlantic multidecadal temperature variability into a forced component and an internal ocean–atmosphere component in a way that is identifiable from the single realization we have, rather than depending on arbitrary detrending choices? And how much predictive information survives in the internal component once the decomposition is fixed?
status: The question has been debated for decades. A 2026 rotated-component analysis (Freveletti et al. 2026, "Multidecadal SST Variability Assessed as Primarily Forced in the Atlantic and Internal in the Pacific Using Rotated Low-Frequency Component Analysis") attributed much of Atlantic variability to forcing, but the decomposition and model assumptions behind such attributions remain consequential.
solved_when: A decomposition method exists whose attribution of Atlantic variability to forcing versus internal dynamics is robust to reasonable changes in its modeling assumptions and detrending choices, together with a quantified measure of the predictive information retained in the internal component.
why: It determines whether decadal predictability claims for the Atlantic rest on a genuine internal mode or on forced signal, and it changes how regional rainfall drivers on multidecadal timescales are interpreted.
key_works: Freveletti et al. (2026), [“Multidecadal SST Variability Assessed as Primarily Forced in the Atlantic and Internal in the Pacific Using Rotated Low-Frequency Component Analysis”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL121516).
aliases: AMV attribution problem; AMO attribution problem.

title: Blocking onset, persistence, and warming response
open: Can we predict when a blocking high will form and how long it will persist, along with the regional warming it produces? A complete theory must account for moist ascent, upstream eddies, stratospheric forcing, and the effects of model resolution on these dynamics.
status: The problem has been studied since the mid-twentieth century, and 2024 experiments — De Luca et al. (2024), ["Enhanced Blocking Frequencies in Very-High Resolution Idealized Climate Model Simulations"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL111016), and Wandel et al. (2024), ["Why Moist Dynamic Processes Matter for the Sub-Seasonal Prediction of Atmospheric Blocking Over Europe"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JD039791) — improved understanding of resolution and moist dynamics but did not eliminate persistent biases.
solved_when: A predictive framework reproduces blocking onset, lifetime, and regional warming response, with the roles of moist ascent, upstream eddies, stratospheric forcing, and resolution quantified and persistent biases eliminated.
why: Blocking highs govern prolonged heatwaves, droughts, cold spells, and stagnation events, so better prediction directly improves sub-seasonal forecasts of the most impactful surface extremes.
key_works: De Luca et al. (2024), [“Enhanced Blocking Frequencies in Very-High Resolution Idealized Climate Model Simulations”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL111016); Wandel et al. (2024), [“Why Moist Dynamic Processes Matter for the Sub-Seasonal Prediction of Atmospheric Blocking Over Europe”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JD039791).

title: Real-world AMOC stability boundary
open: Where, if anywhere, does the real Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) sit relative to a stability boundary? The task is to locate overturning stability thresholds under realistic warming, freshwater forcing, forcing rates, and Southern Ocean coupling, and to determine which of the feedbacks seen in models actually operate in the observed ocean.
status: Multiple equilibria of the overturning have been studied since Stommel’s 1961 model. A 2024 collapse study (van Westen, Kliphuis and Dijkstra, "Physics-based early warning signal shows that AMOC is on tipping course," https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adk1189) and 2025 resilience experiments (Baker et al., "Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes," https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08544-0) produced contrasting conditional results.
solved_when: Stability boundaries of the AMOC are located under realistic warming, freshwater input, forcing rates, and Southern Ocean coupling, with a determination of which modeled feedbacks apply to the observed ocean.
why: A solution constrains the risks that AMOC weakening poses to heat transport, rainfall, and regional sea level.
key_works: van Westen, Kliphuis and Dijkstra (2024), [“Physics-based early warning signal shows that AMOC is on tipping course”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adk1189); Baker et al. (2025), [“Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08544-0).

title: Validated AMOC early-warning observations
open: Which indicators of declining AMOC resilience can actually be observed in the real ocean, and can they provide reliable early warning? In particular, do any candidate indicators have validated lead times, false-alarm rates, and missed-event rates when the proxies are imperfect and the forcing is itself changing?
status: Model-based indicators show promise, but Ben-Yami et al. (2024) demonstrated major obstacles to robustly extrapolating tipping times from historical data, given uncertainties too large for prediction of tipping times of major Earth system components.
solved_when: Directly observable AMOC-resilience indicators exist whose lead times, false-alarm rates, and missed-event rates have been quantitatively validated under realistic imperfect proxies and nonstationary forcing.
why: It would turn a broad concern about AMOC tipping into concrete, testable monitoring requirements — an actionable early-warning system rather than an anxiety.
key_works: Ben-Yami et al. (2024), [“Uncertainties too large to predict tipping times of major Earth system components from historical data”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adl4841).

title: Finite-record limits of AMOC tipping-risk inference
open: How accurately can we estimate the probability that the AMOC tips before a stated horizon, given only a finite observational record of a partially observed, physically constrained stochastic model under prescribed future forcing? Derive tight lower bounds on that estimation error, and identify which observations or assumptions are needed to achieve matching upper bounds.
status: Detection-error tradeoffs were quantified in particular models by 2012, notably by Boettcher–Hastings-style analyses (Boettiger and Hastings, 2012). The sharper physically constrained bounds proposed here remain a formal research target, not an established named conjecture. Related themes appear in Ben-Yami et al. (2024) on uncertainties too large to predict tipping times from historical data and Rietkerk et al. (2025) on the ambiguity of early warning signals.
solved_when: Tight error lower bounds are proven for estimating transition probability before the stated horizon in this setting, and observation/assumption conditions are exhibited under which matching upper bounds hold.
why: It separates reducible uncertainty (fixable with better data or models) from fundamental information limits, telling us when collecting more AMOC observations simply cannot sharpen tipping-risk estimates.
key_works: Boettiger and Hastings (2012), [“Quantifying limits to detection of early warning for critical transitions”](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2012.0125); Ben-Yami et al. (2024), [“Uncertainties too large to predict tipping times of major Earth system components from historical data”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adl4841); Rietkerk et al. (2025), [“Ambiguity of early warning signals for climate tipping points”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-025-02328-8).

title: Antarctic meltwater–abyssal overturning feedback
open: How much does increasing Antarctic meltwater slow the abyssal overturning circulation, and how does that slowdown feed back on the ice shelves themselves through abyssal warming?
status: A 2023 high-resolution projection (Li et al. (2023), ["Abyssal ocean overturning slowdown and warming driven by Antarctic meltwater"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05762-w)) showed substantial meltwater-driven slowdown; coupled ice–ocean modeling and observational constraints remain incomplete.
solved_when: A quantitative, coupled ice–ocean treatment establishes the relationship between meltwater input, dense-water formation, bottom-water export, abyssal warming, and subsequent ice-shelf heat exposure.
why: It determines long-term ocean heat storage and the sea-level commitment of the Antarctic ice sheet.
key_works: Li et al. (2023), [“Abyssal ocean overturning slowdown and warming driven by Antarctic meltwater”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05762-w).

title: State-dependent Southern Ocean eddy compensation
open: Can we predict how strongly mesoscale eddies counteract changes in the wind-driven overturning of the Southern Ocean as the climate changes? The goal is a closure theory in which the degree of eddy compensation is a predicted function of the flow state, incorporating topography, buoyancy forcing, and transient adjustment rather than treating compensation as a fixed fraction.
status: Decades of eddy-resolving experiments establish that compensation is partial, but its strength and its dependence on climate state remain uncertain; Bennetts et al. (2024), ["Closing the Loops on Southern Ocean Dynamics: From the Circumpolar Current to Ice Shelves and From Bottom Mixing to Surface Waves"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022RG000781), survey the coupled dynamics involved.
solved_when: A closure exists that predicts the strength and climate dependence of eddy compensation, explicitly accounting for topography, buoyancy forcing, and transient adjustment, and that reproduces the partial compensation seen in eddy-resolving experiments across climate states.
why: The answer governs how much heat the Southern Ocean takes up and how it responds to shifting winds — a first-order control on projections of Southern Ocean heat uptake.
key_works: Bennetts et al. (2024), [“Closing the Loops on Southern Ocean Dynamics: From the Circumpolar Current to Ice Shelves and From Bottom Mixing to Surface Waves”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022RG000781).

title: Climate effects of submesoscale air–sea coupling
open: Do kilometer-scale ocean fronts, through their air–sea exchanges within storms, accumulate to shape heat fluxes, moisture supply, and atmospheric circulation at climate scale? In particular, can coarse-resolution models be shown to represent these effects correctly across seasons and current systems?
status: A 2025 coupled simulation (Vivant et al. 2025, ["Ocean submesoscale fronts induce diabatic heating and convective precipitation within storms"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02002-z)) identified substantial local heating and precipitation responses; their global climate integral remains unresolved.
solved_when: The accumulated effects of submesoscale fronts on storm heat fluxes, moisture supply, and circulation are quantified, and coarse-model representations are validated across seasons and current systems — including the global climate integral of the local responses.
why: A solution would reveal whether unresolved ocean fronts impose systematic biases in climate models, and how those biases should be corrected.
key_works: Vivant et al. (2025), [“Ocean submesoscale fronts induce diabatic heating and convective precipitation within storms”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02002-z).

title: Predictability of abrupt and subsurface marine heatwaves
open: Can marine heatwaves — including those that develop abruptly or at depth — be forecast with useful skill, in onset, vertical structure, and termination, when the atmosphere shifts rapidly and boundary currents reorganize? The goal is to establish depth-specific limits of predictability and the observing-system requirements needed to reach them.
status: Jacox et al. (2022) demonstrated seasonal forecast skill for surface marine heatwaves, with lead times varying strongly by region; skill for subsurface and abrupt events remains less established.
solved_when: A forecasting framework demonstrates quantified skill for marine-heatwave onset, depth structure, and termination under rapid atmospheric changes and boundary-current shifts, with depth-specific prediction limits and observing requirements established.
why: Advance warning of ocean thermal stress enables protective responses for marine ecosystems and dependent human activities before heatwaves strike.
key_works: Jacox et al. (2022), [“Global seasonal forecasts of marine heatwaves”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04573-9).

title: Basin-specific marine ice-sheet irreversibility
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Which grounding-line retreats in a given Antarctic basin become self-sustaining once started, under realistic buttressing, bed geometry, ocean forcing, and local sea-level feedback? More formally, determine the basin-specific thresholds and rates at which retreat crosses a stabilizing ridge and becomes committed rather than temporary.
status: Instability is well established in idealized settings, beginning with Schoof (2007), ["Ice sheet grounding line dynamics: Steady states, stability, and hysteresis"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006JF000664). The 2025 Antarctic assessment by Fricker et al. (2025), ["Antarctica in 2025: Drivers of deep uncertainty in projected ice loss"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt9619), emphasizes that basin-specific thresholds and retreat rates remain unresolved.
solved_when: For each major basin, there is a determined threshold — grounding-line position or forcing level — beyond which retreat is self-sustaining (committed ridge crossing rather than temporary retreat), together with the associated retreat rates, valid under realistic buttressing, bed geometry, ocean forcing, and local sea-level feedback.
why: It separates ice loss that can still be avoided through mitigation from sea-level rise that is already committed, which is the quantity coastal planners actually need.
key_works: Schoof (2007), [“Ice sheet grounding line dynamics: Steady states, stability, and hysteresis”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006JF000664); Fricker et al. (2025), [“Antarctica in 2025: Drivers of deep uncertainty in projected ice loss”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt9619).

title: Predictive ice-shelf hydrofracture and collapse
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Can the response of an ice shelf to surface meltwater — fracture nucleation, drainage cascades, inherited damage, refreezing, and the evolving stress field — be predicted from physical principles rather than diagnosed after the fact? More precisely, can vulnerability maps be converted into validated probabilities and timescales for shelf collapse?
status: Lai et al. (2020) mapped the vulnerability of Antarctica's ice shelves to meltwater-driven fracture using fracture mechanics, but actual failure timing remains unresolved.
solved_when: A predictive model reproduces meltwater-driven fracture and collapse with quantified probabilities and timescales that are validated against observed shelf failures, accounting for drainage cascades, inherited damage, refreezing, and stress evolution.
why: Ice-shelf collapse removes the buttressing restraint on upstream grounded ice, accelerating its discharge and contributing directly to sea-level rise.
key_works: Lai et al. (2020), [“Vulnerability of Antarctica’s ice shelves to meltwater-driven fracture”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2627-8).

title: Tidal seawater intrusion beneath grounded ice
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Can we directly measure how much heat is exchanged where tidal motion drives seawater into cavities beneath grounded ice? The goal is an observationally validated melt law that predicts ice loss and retreat from the intrusion geometry while resolving subglacial cavities and freshwater drainage.
status: Rignot et al. (2024) observed widespread seawater intrusions beneath the grounded ice of Thwaites Glacier, West Antarctica, but converting the observed geometry into validated melt laws remains open.
solved_when: Heat exchange at tidally forced seawater intrusions beneath grounded ice has been directly measured, and a melt law derived from the observed cavity geometry and drainage has been validated against observed melt and retreat.
why: A validated melt law for these intrusions could explain part of the observed ice retreat that current models underestimate.
key_works: Rignot et al. (2024), [“Widespread seawater intrusions beneath the grounded ice of Thwaites Glacier, West Antarctica”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2404766121).

title: Transferable basal sliding laws
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Can we formulate basal sliding laws whose friction parameters transfer across changing conditions — water pressure, bed roughness, sediment state, and grounding-line geometry — rather than being tuned to reproduce a single velocity snapshot? Formally, the goal is a predictive relation between basal shear stress and sliding velocity that remains valid outside the regime in which its coefficients were inferred.
status: Joughin, Smith and Schoof (2019), ["Regularized Coulomb Friction Laws for Ice Sheet Sliding: Application to Pine Island Glacier, Antarctica"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019GL082526), improved Pine Island Glacier evolution simulations using regularized Coulomb friction; however, transferability of friction parameters across bed and drainage regimes remains unresolved.
solved_when: A sliding law is demonstrated to predict ice velocity or discharge under conditions (water pressure, roughness, sediment, grounding geometry) materially different from those used to infer its friction coefficients, with validation beyond a single velocity snapshot.
why: Basal friction strongly controls ice-discharge responses, so a non-transferable law undermines predictions of how ice sheets evolve under forcing.
key_works: Joughin, Smith and Schoof (2019), [“Regularized Coulomb Friction Laws for Ice Sheet Sliding: Application to Pine Island Glacier, Antarctica”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019GL082526).

title: Greenland overshoot-duration boundary
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Which combinations of peak warming, overshoot duration, and subsequent cooling commit the Greenland ice sheet to irreversible large-scale ice loss? A full answer would characterize a boundary in (peak temperature, duration, cooling) space, accounting for regional forcing and dynamical uncertainty in the ice sheet's response.
status: Bochow et al. (2023) demonstrated strong pathway dependence in two models; no universally measured tipping-temperature boundary follows.
solved_when: A quantified boundary in the space of peak warming, overshoot duration, and cooling is established that separates reversible from irreversible large ice loss for Greenland, valid under regional forcing and robust to dynamic uncertainty.
why: Similar final stabilized temperatures can imply very different long-term sea levels, so pathway details — not just end-state warming — determine whether Greenland's ice loss is locked in.
key_works: Bochow et al. (2023), [“Overshooting the critical threshold for the Greenland ice sheet”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06503-9).

title: Evolving debris, cliffs, and ponds on mountain glaciers
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Can we predict the total melt from a debris-covered mountain glacier as its debris layer thickens and its ice cliffs and ponds evolve over time? why: Debris, cliff, and pond evolution controls whether a glacier survives, how much seasonal water supply it delivers, and the hazards it poses downstream.

why: The cutoff governs where the scale-invariant regime terminates, which controls ice hazards and heat exchange through leads.

title: Calibrated probability of Arctic ice-free conditions
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: What is the actual probability that the Arctic Ocean becomes ice-free — on a first day, over a first month, or recurrently across a season — below a specified ice-area threshold? Such an estimate should separate the contributions of emissions scenario, structural model bias, and weather-driven timing uncertainty.

solved_when: Calibrated first-day, first-month, and recurrent-season probabilities below the specified ice-free threshold are produced, with scenario effects, structural bias, and weather-driven timing uncertainty separately quantified.
why: It distinguishes isolated low-ice events from persistent summer ice-free regimes, which matter very differently for ecosystems, shipping, and feedbacks.

title: Regional dynamical amplification of extreme precipitation
open: Where in the world will the atmosphere's circulation and storm dynamics amplify — or suppress — the rainfall intensification that simple thermodynamics predicts? The goal is a theory explaining how circulation, vertical motion, stability, and precipitation efficiency jointly shape regional rainfall extremes, yielding local return-level changes across durations.
status: Pfahl et al. (2017) separated modeled thermodynamic and dynamical contributions, but uncertain circulation and unresolved processes still limit regional estimates.
solved_when: A quantitative account exists that predicts, region by region and across durations, how dynamical factors modulate thermodynamic rainfall increases, expressed as local changes in precipitation return levels.
why: These regional return-level changes set the design loads for drainage systems and flood protection, so getting the dynamical amplification right determines whether infrastructure is over- or under-built.
key_works: Pfahl, O’Gorman and Fischer (2017), [“Understanding the regional pattern of projected future changes in extreme precipitation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate3287).

title: Tail dependence of compound heat and drought
open: Can we estimate how the joint probabilities, persistence, and spatial synchronization of heat, precipitation deficits, and soil-moisture depletion will change in a future climate? Formally, the challenge is to characterize the tail dependence structure among these variables and to validate inferred changes in that dependence beyond the range of the observed record.
status: Multivariate extreme-value frameworks expanded substantially in the 2010s (Zscheischler et al. (2018), ["Future climate risk from compound events"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-018-0156-3)), but sparse extremes and nonstationarity still obstruct high-return-period estimates.

open: When methanogenesis in the rumen is inhibited, the hydrogen that methanogens would normally consume must go somewhere — can it be redirected into useful fermentation products rather than being expelled as gas or disrupting digestion? The goal is to establish stable interventions, verified by whole-animal energy balances, that channel these reducing equivalents productively.
status: Lopes et al. (2016) documented hydrogen and fermentation responses to 3-nitrooxypropanol in dairy cows, but efficient recovery of feed-energy benefits remains unresolved.
solved_when: A stable intervention is demonstrated in which inhibiting rumen methanogenesis redirects hydrogen into useful fermentation products, with whole-animal energy balances confirming efficient recovery of the feed energy otherwise lost.
why: Success would improve both emissions outcomes and feed conversion efficiency in ruminant livestock.
key_works: Lopes et al. (2016), [“Effect of 3-nitrooxypropanol on methane and hydrogen emissions, methane isotopic signature, and ruminal fermentation in dairy cows”](https://doi.org/10.3168/jds.2015-10832).

title: Rice water management with a complete greenhouse-gas budget
open: Can rice water management — the coordinated choice of wetting–drying schedule, nitrogen inputs, and residue handling — preserve yield while lowering the full greenhouse-gas footprint of a paddy, including CH₄, N₂O, and soil-carbon effects, under the irrigation constraints farms actually face?
status: Liu et al. (2024) demonstrated management co-benefits in ["Co-benefits for net carbon emissions and rice yields through improved management of organic nitrogen and water"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-024-00940-z), but site dependence and coordination requirements prevent universal prescriptions.
solved_when: A jointly optimized management package is demonstrated at farm scale that maintains yield relative to standard practice while measurably reducing combined CH₄, N₂O, and soil-carbon impacts under real irrigation constraints.
why: It would turn successful plot-scale treatments into reliable, repeatable greenhouse-gas reductions across working rice farms.
key_works: Liu et al. (2024), [“Co-benefits for net carbon emissions and rice yields through improved management of organic nitrogen and water”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-024-00940-z).

title: Affordable measurement of small soil-carbon changes
open: Can management-induced changes in soil carbon be detected affordably and reliably against the noise of heterogeneous background stocks? Concretely, this asks for validation of hybrid schemes that combine field sampling, spectroscopy, and models on independent long-term sites.
status: Smith et al. (2020) outlined integrated measurement, reporting, and verification for soil carbon change, but expensive sampling and slow detectable change remain the central obstacles.
solved_when: A hybrid sampling–spectroscopy–modeling approach is validated on independent long-term sites and demonstrably detects management effects at a cost proportionate to the small changes being measured.
why: Without affordable detection, verification stays expensive and slow, excluding small farms; with it, credible carbon accounting becomes practical at farm scale.
key_works: Smith et al. (2020), [“How to measure, report and verify soil carbon change to realize the potential of soil carbon sequestration for atmospheric greenhouse gas removal”](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.14815).

title: Perennial-grain performance through repeated stress and harvest
open: Can a perennial grain crop sustain multiyear yields competitive with annuals while the pests, weeds, and nutrient limitations that accumulate across repeated stress and harvest cycles are kept under control — and do so with durable net climate benefits across varying soils and input regimes?
status: Zhang et al. (2023; online 2022) demonstrated sustained perennial-rice productivity; transferring this performance to other grains and environments remains open.
solved_when: A perennial grain system demonstrates competitive multiyear grain yield under repeated stress and harvest, with accumulated pest, weed, and nutrient constraints controlled, and verified durable net climate benefits that hold across different soils and input levels.
why: Success would reduce soil disturbance and labor while improving resilience of grain production systems.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2023), [“Sustained productivity and agronomic potential of perennial rice”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-022-00997-3).

title: Crop failure under compound reproductive-stage extremes
open: Can we predict how heat, drought, excess rainfall, and nutrient stress interact when they strike crops during flowering and grain filling — the stages where yield is most vulnerable? More precisely, can models of compound reproductive-stage extremes be validated beyond the range of historical climates and distinguish physiological responses from management adaptation?
status: Jägermeyr et al. (2021), ["Climate impacts on global agriculture emerge earlier in new generation of climate and crop models"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-021-00400-y), found substantial shifts in projected impacts across model generations; local losses from compound events remain uncertain.
solved_when: A predictive framework captures the interacting effects of heat, drought, excess-rainfall, and nutrient stress during flowering and grain filling, validated out of sample beyond historical climate conditions, and shown to separate physiological from management-driven adaptation.
why: Compound-event losses at local scale remain a major uncertainty in food-security projections, and resolving them would directly guide resilient breeding and food-system planning.
key_works: Jägermeyr et al. (2021), [“Climate impacts on global agriculture emerge earlier in new generation of climate and crop models”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-021-00400-y).

title: Preventing crop nutrient dilution under elevated CO₂
open: Can we prevent the declines in protein, zinc, iron, and other nutrients that crops suffer under elevated CO₂, without sacrificing yield even under heat and water stress — and can such cultivars be validated across varied soils and dietary contexts?
status: Myers et al. (2014), in ["Increasing CO₂ threatens human nutrition"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13179), documented nutrient declines under elevated CO₂ and variation among cultivars; broadly effective prevention remains unresolved.
solved_when: Cultivars are identified that maintain protein, zinc, iron, and other nutrient levels under elevated CO₂ while sustaining yields under heat and water stress, and this performance is validated across diverse soils and diets.
why: It protects human nutrition beyond mere calorie availability as CO₂ rises.
key_works: Myers et al. (2014), [“Increasing CO₂ threatens human nutrition”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13179).

title: Low-cost DAC measured per net tonne stored
open: Can direct air capture deliver durable carbon removal at a fully accounted cost below a declared target, such as US$100 per net tonne of CO₂ stored? The target must include all energy, financing, water, materials, transport, and storage costs, sustained in continuous operation rather than as a point estimate.
status: Keith et al. (2018) supplied an engineering cost basis, and Deutz and Bardow (2021) quantified lifecycle burdens, but existing estimates do not establish continuous delivery costs.
solved_when: A demonstrated DAC system shows sustained delivery of durable removal at a total cost per net tonne stored below the declared target (e.g., US$100), with the accounting covering energy, finance, water, materials, transport, and storage.
why: Without demonstrated full-cost delivery, large-scale removal commitments rest on engineering estimates rather than evidence; achieving it makes those commitments financially and physically credible.
key_works: Keith et al. (2018), [“A Process for Capturing CO₂ from the Atmosphere”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2018.05.006); Deutz and Bardow (2021), [“Life-cycle assessment of an industrial direct air capture process based on temperature–vacuum swing adsorption”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-00771-9).

title: Long-life electrochemical direct air capture

solved_when: A demonstration shows multiyear-equivalent durability at useful capture throughput, with complete energy and materials balances reported.
why: It would enable modular, electrically regenerated CO₂ capture as a deployable carbon-removal technology rather than a lab-scale curiosity.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), [“Redox-decoupled electrolysis for direct air capture of CO₂”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44286-026-00391-2).

title: Weathering dissolution-to-removal conversion at watershed scale
open: When basalt or other silicate rock dissolves, how much of the released alkalinity actually survives the journey through soils, secondary mineral phases, groundwater, and rivers to reach the ocean? Quantifying this dissolution-to-removal conversion at the watershed scale — and separating the various acid sources along the way so that mass balances linking rock dissolution to atmospheric CO₂ removal can be closed — remains unmeasured.
status: Derry, Maher and Chadwick (2026) documented attenuation of alkalinity export in natural basaltic watersheds in "Critical zone processes limit alkalinity export from natural basaltic systems" (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10936-3); losses under engineered application remain unvalidated.
solved_when: Watershed-scale measurements trace alkalinity from rock dissolution through soils, secondary minerals, groundwater, and rivers, with acid sources separated and mass balances closed, so that the fraction of dissolved alkalinity converted to durable atmospheric removal is quantified; engineered-application losses must also be validated.
why: Dissolved cations alone cannot certify removal — without knowing how much alkalinity survives transit to the ocean, enhanced weathering claims cannot be verified or credited.
key_works: Derry, Maher and Chadwick (2026), [“Critical zone processes limit alkalinity export from natural basaltic systems”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10936-3).

title: Weathering feedstocks with verified long-term agronomic safety
open: Can enhanced weathering feedstocks be applied repeatedly while keeping nickel, chromium, and other contaminants from accumulating to levels that harm crops or food safety — and how does their bioavailability evolve as soil chemistry shifts over years of application?
status: Trials show site-specific benefits; Beerling et al. (2025) identify long-term environmental evaluation and feedstock variability as key scaling challenges.
solved_when: Field trials demonstrate net carbon dioxide removal with contaminant (e.g., nickel, chromium) accumulation held within acceptable agronomic and food-quality thresholds across repeated applications, under changing soil chemistry and accounting for feedstock variability.
why: Without verified long-term safety, weathering deployments risk contaminating soils, food crops, and downstream ecosystems, undermining a major CDR pathway's social license to scale.
key_works: Beerling et al. (2025), [“Challenges and opportunities in scaling enhanced weathering for carbon dioxide removal”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-025-00713-7).

title: Ecological limits of repeated ocean alkalinity exposure
open: What happens to marine organisms and communities when they experience ocean alkalinity enhancement plumes repeatedly rather than once? Experiments are needed that disentangle the effects of pH change, introduced impurities, nutrient shifts, and carbonate chemistry, and that identify measurable endpoints which predict population-level outcomes in open ecosystems.
status: Marín-Samper et al. (2024) found no inferred damaging metabolism response within their tested CO₂-equilibrated range; broader exposure conditions remain unresolved.
solved_when: Repeated-exposure experiments exist that separately attribute observed responses to pH, impurities, nutrients, and carbonate chemistry, and validate experimental endpoints as predictors of population outcomes in open ecosystems.
why: It defines the deployment envelopes within which OAE can operate effectively and the monitoring indicators needed to detect ecological harm before it scales.
key_works: Marín-Samper et al. (2024), [“Assessing the impact of CO₂-equilibrated ocean alkalinity enhancement on microbial metabolic rates in an oligotrophic system”](https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-21-2859-2024).

title: Additional atmospheric removal from cultivated seaweed
open: When seaweed is cultivated for carbon removal, how much atmospheric CO₂ is genuinely removed beyond what the unperturbed ecosystem would have absorbed? A rigorous answer requires measuring uptake after accounting for phytoplankton competition for nutrients, calcifying epibionts, and delayed air–sea equilibration, and establishing additionality against a no-farming counterfactual.
status: Bach et al. (2021) quantified possible deductions from the removal potential of seaweed afforestation, and subsequent published exchanges have contested the generality of those findings; system-specific measured additionality remains open.
solved_when: A system-specific, measured additionality estimate exists for a cultivated seaweed operation — i.e., net atmospheric uptake quantified after deductions for phytoplankton competition, nutrient limitation, calcifying epibionts, and delayed equilibration, relative to the ecosystem baseline without farming.
why: It distinguishes true atmospheric carbon removal from mere redistribution of ocean productivity, determining whether seaweed farming delivers real climate benefit.
key_works: Bach et al. (2021), [“Testing the climate intervention potential of ocean afforestation using the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22837-2).

title: Biochar permanence across feedstocks and environments
open: Can we predict how quickly a given biochar will decay, and how it will affect native soil carbon, from its production conditions and material properties alone, across the range of environments where it is applied? Formally, this asks for validated models of century-scale carbon retention built on observations and defensible aging relationships.
status: Woolf et al. (2010), ["Sustainable biochar to mitigate global climate change"](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms1053), quantified the sustainable potential of biochar; Lehmann et al. (2021), ["Biochar in climate change mitigation"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8), synthesized the persistent, system-dependent durability uncertainties that remain unresolved.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that forecasts biochar decay and native-carbon effects from production and material properties across environments, and whose century-scale retention estimates are validated against observations through defensible aging relationships.
why: It enables credible carbon accounting across heterogeneous pyrolysis products, so removals credited today can be trusted over the timescales they are claimed for.
key_works: Woolf et al. (2010), [“Sustainable biochar to mitigate global climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms1053); Lehmann et al. (2021), [“Biochar in climate change mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8).

title: Engineered wood burial with demonstrable durability
open: Can we design a low-cost engineered wood burial system that suppresses decomposition and methane production across varying wood types, hydrological conditions, and geologies — and can we detect deteriorating protective conditions before substantial carbon reversal occurs?
status: Zeng et al. (2024) examined a 3,775-year-old preserved log in ["3775-year-old wood burial supports 'wood vaulting' as a durable carbon removal method"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adm8133); reproducing that preservation at engineered scale remains empirical.
solved_when: A burial design demonstrates suppressed decomposition and methane emissions at engineered scale across wood, hydrology, and geology, together with a monitoring capability that identifies protective-condition failure before substantial reversal of stored carbon.
why: It would allow durable storage of sustainable biomass with little processing energy, making wood vaulting a credible low-cost carbon dioxide removal method.
key_works: Zeng et al. (2024), [“3775-year-old wood burial supports ‘wood vaulting’ as a durable carbon removal method”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adm8133).

title: BECCS potential under simultaneous land and water constraints
open: How much net CO₂ can bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) actually remove if land and water limits are enforced at the same time? A satisfactory answer must preserve environmental flows, groundwater, ecosystems, and food production while accounting for land-use counterfactuals and supply-chain emissions.
status: Ai et al. (2021) found that sustainable irrigation sharply limits unconstrained BECCS potential; how land and water constraints interact remains scenario dependent.
solved_when: A quantified estimate of net-removal capacity is obtained under simultaneous land and water constraints that maintain environmental flows, groundwater, ecosystems, and food production, with land-use counterfactuals and supply-chain emissions included.
why: It tests whether the removal levels assumed in mitigation pathways are physically available; without it, pathway reliance on BECCS may rest on capacity that vanishes once resource constraints bind.
key_works: Ai et al. (2021), [“Global bioenergy with carbon capture and storage potential is largely constrained by sustainable irrigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-021-00740-4).

title: Full climate benefit of forest restoration
open: Can we predict how forest restoration changes climate over time once all the main biophysical pathways — carbon uptake, surface albedo, evapotranspiration, cloud effects, and disturbance regimes — act together? A satisfactory answer would yield time-dependent warming curves and spatial recommendations that hold up across forest types.
status: Hasler et al. (2024) mapped carbon–albedo accounting in ["Accounting for albedo change to identify climate-positive tree cover restoration"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46577-1); the cloud, hydrological, and disturbance contributions remain uncertain.
solved_when: A validated model exists that combines carbon, albedo, evapotranspiration, cloud, and disturbance effects to predict time-dependent warming from restoration, and its spatial recommendations are validated across forest types.
why: It would identify restoration projects that deliver genuine climate benefits rather than ones whose biophysical side effects offset or reverse their carbon gains.
key_works: Hasler et al. (2024), [“Accounting for albedo change to identify climate-positive tree cover restoration”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46577-1).

title: Forecasting correlated reversal of restored forest carbon
open: Can we forecast the joint risk that fire, drought, insects, and disease reverse carbon stored in forest restoration portfolios, given that these disturbances are correlated rather than independent? Formally, the task is to estimate the distribution of combined disturbance losses across a portfolio and to identify species mixtures and spatial designs that maximize carbon retained over multiple decades.
status: Anderegg et al. (2022) mapped US forest risks from stress, insects, and fire (["Future climate risks from stress, insects and fire across US forests"](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.14018)); correlated disturbances and unfamiliar climates complicate durability forecasting.
solved_when: A method exists for estimating joint fire, drought, insect, and disease losses across restoration portfolios at multi-decadal horizons, together with demonstrated portfolio mixtures and spatial designs that improve retained carbon relative to unspecified baselines under correlated disturbance risk.
why: Geographically dispersed restoration projects can still fail together under correlated disturbances, so carbon-credit durability and portfolio planning that assumes independence can break down exactly when it matters most.
key_works: Anderegg et al. (2022), [“Future climate risks from stress, insects and fire across US forests”](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.14018).

title: Peatland rewetting with controlled methane trajectories
open: Can peatland water tables and vegetation communities be managed so that rewetting halts peat oxidation without triggering avoidable methane pulses — and can wet conditions be maintained through drought, with recovery trajectories quantified?
status: Günther et al. (2020) showed prompt rewetting can reduce warming despite methane emissions; site-specific optimization of water tables and vegetation remains open.
solved_when: A management strategy for water tables and vegetation is demonstrated that stops peat oxidation, limits avoidable methane emissions, sustains wet conditions through drought, and yields quantified methane and carbon recovery trajectories.
why: It would let restoration projects capture the full climate benefit of rewetting while ending the ongoing CO₂ losses from drained peat.
key_works: Günther et al. (2020), [“Prompt rewetting of drained peatlands reduces climate warming despite methane emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-15499-z).

title: Coastal blue-carbon persistence under wetland migration
open: Can we predict how much coastal blue carbon is retained when marshes and mangroves erode, accrete, migrate inland, or drown under rising seas? A satisfying answer must resolve the roles of sediment supply, migration barriers, and the ultimate fate of eroded carbon.
status: Campbell et al. (2022) mapped global marsh changes and associated carbon emissions in ["Global hotspots of salt marsh change and carbon emissions"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05355-z); complete future carbon budgets remain difficult.
solved_when: A predictive framework yields complete future carbon budgets for migrating coastal wetlands, accounting for sediment supply, barriers to migration, and the fate of eroded carbon.
why: It would make coastal restoration carbon accounting robust to moving shorelines, so credited sequestration is not lost when habitats shift or erode.
key_works: Campbell et al. (2022), [“Global hotspots of salt marsh change and carbon emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05355-z).
