title: Physiological heat limits across real populations
open: How hot can environments get before human physiology can no longer compensate — and how does that limit shift across real populations rather than idealized subjects? Specifically, determine heat-compensation limits as functions of age, health status, exertion, humidity, radiation, airflow, clothing, and exposure duration, so that population risk can be assessed without relying on a universal wet-bulb threshold.
status: Vecellio et al. (2022) experimentally challenged the 35°C wet-bulb adaptability threshold in young, healthy adults (PSU HEAT Project, ["Evaluating the 35°C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects"](https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00738.2021)); whether those findings transfer to broader populations remains unresolved.
solved_when: Experimentally validated heat-compensation limits are established across the variables named (age, health, exertion, humidity, radiation, airflow, clothing, and duration), enabling population-level risk assessment that does not assume a single universal wet-bulb threshold such as 35°C.
why: It supports realistic estimates of habitability limits and adaptation capacity, replacing an idealized threshold with transferable, population-specific physiological limits for climate impact assessment.
key_works: Vecellio et al. (2022), [“Evaluating the 35°C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects (PSU HEAT Project)”](https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00738.2021).

title: Causal limits to adaptation in temperature-related mortality
open: How much of the mortality burden from extreme heat and cold can actually be prevented through income growth, infrastructure, behavioral change, and public health — and when we project mortality under temperatures never before observed, how do we causally separate true adaptation from the confounding effects of migration and population composition?
status: Carleton et al. (2022), in "Valuing the Global Mortality Consequences of Climate Change Accounting for Adaptation Costs and Benefits," incorporated adaptation costs and benefits into mortality projections, but causal extrapolation beyond the observed temperature range remains uncertain.
solved_when: A causal framework can be given that quantifies the mortality reduction attributable to each adaptation channel (income, infrastructure, behavior, public health) and yields projections of temperature-related mortality under unprecedented heat that are demonstrably robust to migration and composition effects.
why: It determines how much health damage from climate change is preventable and what resources adaptation would require, informing both mitigation benefit estimates and adaptation investment decisions.
key_works: Carleton et al. (2022), [“Valuing the Global Mortality Consequences of Climate Change Accounting for Adaptation Costs and Benefits”](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/137/4/2037/6571943).

title: Urban greening that reduces actual unequal heat exposure
open: Which urban greening interventions — plantings, parks, green space — actually reduce people's personal heat exposure and heat-related illness across income groups, once humidity, nighttime heat, water needs, accessibility, and displacement risks are accounted for?
status: Li et al. (2024) mapped cooling inequalities globally; exposure-level and causal health evidence remains less complete.
solved_when: There is exposure-level, causal evidence identifying intervention types that reduce heat exposure and illness across income groups, incorporating humidity, nighttime heat, water, accessibility, and displacement.
why: It targets adaptation spending toward actual risk reduction rather than assumed cooling benefits.
key_works: Li et al. (2024), [“Green spaces provide substantial but unequal urban cooling globally”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-51355-0).

title: Climate-sensitive mosquito transmission beyond thermal suitability
open: Can we predict the transmission of mosquito-borne pathogens that actually occurs in a population, once immunity, vector adaptation, human mobility, housing conditions, and intervention efforts are considered alongside climate? A sharper formulation asks whether mechanistic temperature–transmission relationships can be validated when transplanted to climates and locations beyond those where they were fitted.
status: Mordecai et al. (2017) linked thermal traits to observed transmission of Zika, dengue, and chikungunya using mechanistic models; however, projections of future case burdens remain conditioned on changing social and biological systems, which are not yet captured.
solved_when: A validated model predicts realized transmission in new climates and locations while explicitly accounting for immunity, vector adaptation, mobility, housing, and control, and its mechanistic temperature relationships hold out of sample.
why: It converts climate projections into concrete prevention priorities, telling decision-makers where and when intervention will matter rather than where temperature alone permits transmission.
key_works: Mordecai et al. (2017), [“Detecting the impact of temperature on transmission of Zika, dengue, and chikungunya using mechanistic models”](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0005568).

title: Chronic wildfire-smoke exposure and protective interventions
open: What are the long-term health effects of repeated exposure to wildfire-smoke seasons, and which interventions actually reduce that exposure and the disease that follows? Answering this requires accounting for smoke chemistry, indoor infiltration, behavioral avoidance, and the concurrent heat that accompanies smoke events.
status: Burke et al. (2021) linked changing fire to exposure and identified substantial chronic-dose and intervention uncertainties; the long-term dose–response and protective-intervention evidence remains open.
solved_when: We have credible estimates of the chronic health effects of repeated seasonal smoke exposure that disentangle chemical composition, infiltration, avoidance behavior, and co-occurring heat, plus demonstrated interventions that measurably reduce exposure and subsequent disease.
why: Wildfire smoke imposes health burdens on populations far beyond the burned areas themselves, so these estimates determine how large and how widespread the true health cost of a changing fire regime is.
key_works: Burke et al. (2021), [“The changing risk and burden of wildfire in the United States”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2011048118).

title: Coral adaptation rates that preserve functioning reefs
open: How fast can coral tolerance to heat actually rise through acclimatization, natural selection, symbiont shuffling, or assisted evolution — and can that gain be achieved without costing the coral its ability to reproduce? A sharper version asks whether such adaptation persists and accumulates across repeated heatwave events rather than a single episode.
status: Lachs et al. (2023) inferred rising thermal tolerance in Palau corals, but whether adaptation rates are sufficient across reef systems remains unestablished.
solved_when: Adaptation rates are quantified for each mechanism, shown not to impair reproduction, and demonstrated to persist through repeated heatwaves at levels sufficient to maintain functioning reefs across reef systems.
why: It defines where restoration can maintain functioning reefs; without knowing these rates, intervention effort cannot be matched to realistic adaptive capacity.
key_works: Lachs et al. (2023), [“Emergent increase in coral thermal tolerance reduces mass bleaching under climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-40601-6).

title: Adaptive management of shifting transboundary fish stocks
open: Can harvest and allocation rules for transboundary fish stocks be designed to remain sustainable and politically stable as climate-driven range shifts move populations across jurisdictional boundaries — formally, can agreements and biological stock boundaries be updated adaptively fast enough that historical allocations do not fail before renegotiation occurs?
status: Palacios-Abrantes et al. (2022) projected shifts in shared stocks and showed they challenge existing management; implementable adaptive allocation remains unresolved.
solved_when: A set of harvest and allocation rules is specified that provably remains sustainable and politically stable as stocks cross jurisdictions, together with a mechanism for updating biological stock boundaries and agreements ahead of the failure of historical allocations.
why: Without such rules, shifting stocks undermine fisheries management, threaten food supplies, and can break down international cooperation over shared resources.
key_works: Palacios-Abrantes et al. (2022), [“Timing and magnitude of climate-driven range shifts in transboundary fish stocks challenge their management”](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16058).

title: Comparable causal evidence of adaptation effectiveness
open: How much do real-world adaptation actions actually reduce climate losses, compared to a counterfactual without them? We seek representative causal evidence covering outcome distributions, costs, durability over time, and failures such as maladaptation or performance under later climate change.
status: Berrang-Ford et al. (2021), in a systematic global stocktake of evidence on human adaptation to climate change, identified gaps in effectiveness, geographical, and temporal coverage of the evidence base.
solved_when: There exists a representative body of causal evidence quantifying loss reduction against counterfactuals, including distributional outcomes, costs, and duration of effectiveness, and explicitly documenting failures and maladaptation.
why: It would let adaptation budgets be allocated toward interventions with demonstrated outcomes, rather than assumed ones.
key_works: Berrang-Ford et al. (2021), [“A systematic global stocktake of evidence on human adaptation to climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-021-01170-y).

title: Durable and equitable outcomes of managed retreat
open: Can managed retreat be designed so that relocated households keep their housing, livelihoods, social networks, and decision-making agency while genuinely reducing lifetime exposure to hazard — and how do outcomes differ across receiving locations, renters, and households excluded from programs?
status: Mach et al. (2019) analyzed over 40,000 US buyouts; the subsequent wellbeing and risk distributions remain less documented.
solved_when: Empirical evidence documents the post-relocation distribution of wellbeing and residual risk across households — including receiving locations, renters, and excluded households — sufficient to distinguish relocation designs that preserve housing, livelihoods, networks, and agency from those that transfer risk or hide losses.
why: Without such evidence, relocation programs can silently shift hazard exposure and displace losses onto renters and excluded households rather than reduce them.
key_works: Mach et al. (2019), [“Managed retreat through voluntary buyouts of flood-prone properties”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aax8995).

title: Aquifer recovery under intensifying climate variability
open: What combinations of pumping limits, recharge efforts, allocation rules, and land management can return a depleted aquifer to recovery without sacrificing the ecosystems and livelihoods that depend on it? A satisfactory answer should hold under changing climate extremes and account for subsidence and water-quality degradation.
status: Jasechko et al. (2024) analyzed about 170,000 wells and documented both decline and recovery cases globally, but transferable recovery rules remain open.
solved_when: A theory (or empirically transferable rule set) identifies management combinations under which aquifer recovery is achieved while ecosystems and livelihoods are protected, with changing extremes, subsidence, and water quality explicitly incorporated.
why: It determines whether groundwater can remain a reliable buffer against intensifying drought; without transferable recovery rules, depletion may become effectively irreversible via subsidence and quality loss.
key_works: Jasechko et al. (2024), [“Rapid groundwater decline and some cases of recovery in aquifers globally”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06879-8).

title: Thirty-year perovskite–silicon tandem reliability
open: Can perovskite–silicon tandem solar cells be designed, and their aging modeled, so that their 30-year outdoor energy yield is reliably predicted across climates, including coupled degradation modes and quantified uncertainty?
status: Open since the 2010s. Efficient devices and outdoor trials exist, but the 2024 roadmap (Alberi et al. (2024), ["A roadmap for tandem photovoltaics"](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2024.01.017)) still lists lifetime qualification as unresolved.
solved_when: Validated designs and accelerated-aging models exist that predict 30-year outdoor energy yield across climates, accounting for coupled degradation and uncertainty, and lifetime qualification is thereby resolved.
why: Higher tandem efficiency only matters commercially if it translates into competitive lifetime electricity cost.
key_works: Alberi et al. (2024), [“A roadmap for tandem photovoltaics”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2024.01.017).

title: Manufacturing tandems without a scale-up efficiency penalty
open: Can tandem photovoltaic modules be manufactured at large scale while keeping the efficiency already achieved in small laboratory cells? Formally, this means achieving reproducible deposition of all layers, reliable interconnection, current matching, and adequate yield and throughput on full-size modules without the efficiency penalty that currently separates production devices from research cells.
status: Laboratory efficiencies establish the potential of tandem photovoltaics, but scalable deposition and manufacturing integration remain open gaps identified in the 2024 roadmap (Alberi et al. (2024), ["A roadmap for tandem photovoltaics"](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2024.01.017)).
solved_when: Large-area modules are produced with reproducible layers, interconnection, current matching, yield, and throughput at manufacturing scale, while retaining small-device laboratory efficiency.
why: It converts record research-cell performance into affordable, mass-produced modules, which is the step that actually affects electricity costs and deployment.
key_works: Alberi et al. (2024), [“A roadmap for tandem photovoltaics”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2024.01.017).

title: Predicting light-induced halide segregation
open: Can we predict when light exposure will drive halide segregation in mixed-halide perovskites, and design compositions that resist it? A successful theory should forecast segregation under combined light, bias, strain, and temperature, and its predictions should be validated on new materials.

why: Light-induced segregation undermines the wide-bandgap absorbers needed for tandem solar cells, so reliable prediction is what turns tandem design from trial-and-error into engineering.

title: Atmospheric replenishment and large wind-farm wakes
open: Can we predict how the atmosphere replenishes the momentum extracted by large wind farms when neighboring wakes interact, across atmospheric stability, passing fronts, complex terrain, and offshore transitions? The goal is a validated theory of momentum recovery spanning scales from individual turbines up to regionally dense deployment.
status: Decades of wake research and steering demonstrations provide partial control over wakes, but atmosphere–plant coupling remains a named grand challenge (Veers et al. (2019), ["Grand challenges in the science of wind energy"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aau2027)).
solved_when: A predictive model of wake interaction and momentum recovery is validated across the full range of conditions named (stability, fronts, terrain, offshore transitions) and across scales from turbine level to regional deployment density.
why: It determines regional wind resource potential, required farm spacing, and projected revenues — the quantities that govern how much electricity wind can actually supply.
key_works: Veers et al. (2019), [“Grand challenges in the science of wind energy”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aau2027).

title: Floating-wind fatigue under coupled extremes
open: How should floating offshore wind platforms be designed jointly — platform, moorings, turbine, and control system together — when wind, wave, and current loads are correlated and extremes dominate? The question sharpens into validating lifetime fatigue estimates for turbines larger than today's commercial machines under such coupled conditions.
status: Commercial floating turbines are already operating, but a 2023 assessment (Veers et al. 2023, ["Grand challenges in the design, manufacture, and operation of future wind turbine systems"](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-8-1071-2023)) still lists coupled dynamics, scaling to larger machines, and validated design models as open research needs.
solved_when: An integrated design methodology exists that co-designs platform, moorings, turbine, and controls under correlated wind–wave–current extreme loading, with lifetime fatigue validated across larger machines than currently deployed.
why: It would cut overdesigned structures and the costly offshore failures that plague floating wind economics.
key_works: Veers et al. (2023), [“Grand challenges in the design, manufacture, and operation of future wind turbine systems”](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-8-1071-2023).

title: Wildlife-aware wind-plant control
open: Can wind plants detect vulnerable wildlife early enough to steer turbine operation away from harm, and can such curtailment be shown to deliver measurable population-level benefits at a bounded energy cost?
status: Curtailment, radar, cameras, and acoustics provide partial solutions; environmental co-design is explicit in the 2022 research agenda [Veers et al. (2022), "Grand Challenges: wind energy research needs for a global energy transition"](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-7-2491-2022).
solved_when: Detection-and-response is demonstrated across species, seasons, and visibility conditions, with quantified population benefits and quantified energy costs.
why: It reduces biodiversity harm from wind development while reducing project-permitting uncertainty for operators.
key_works: Veers et al. (2022), [“Grand Challenges: wind energy research needs for a global energy transition”](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-7-2491-2022).

title: Decades-long engineered geothermal reservoir productivity
open: Can an engineered geothermal reservoir be operated so that distributed flow is sustained for decades without early thermal breakthrough, excessive water loss, or rapid productivity decline? More formally, can we predict and control multi-decade heat recovery across varying geologies?
status: The problem has been pursued since 1970s hot-dry-rock programs. Horizontal drilling and multizone stimulation have improved field demonstrations, notably in DOE's FORGE multizone-stimulation results (2024) and its Subsurface Enhancement and Sustainability program, but how such reservoirs evolve over their lifetime remains uncertain.
solved_when: A reservoir design and operation strategy is demonstrated that maintains distributed flow over decades-long horizons while avoiding early thermal breakthrough, excessive water loss, and rapid output decline, with predictive capability for heat recovery across diverse geologies.
why: It would establish geothermal as a financeable source of firm, low-carbon electricity, since lenders require decades of predictable output before committing capital.
key_works: U.S. DOE, [“Subsurface Enhancement and Sustainability”](https://www.energy.gov/hgeo/geothermal/subsurface-enhancement-and-sustainability); DOE (2024), [FORGE multizone-stimulation results](https://www.energy.gov/hgeo/geothermal/forge).

title: Repeatable advanced-reactor construction economics
open: Can a standardized advanced-reactor program be built repeatedly on predictable schedules with independently documented cost declines that include financing and site work — and can we determine the conditions under which modularization beats the scale economies it gives up?
status: The question has been debated for decades; DOE's 2024 assessment identifies orderbooks, first-project risk, and construction execution as the key barriers [U.S. DOE (2024), "Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear—Update"](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/LIFTOFF_DOE_Advanced-Nuclear-Update.pdf).
solved_when: A standardized project series demonstrates predictable schedules and independently documented cost reductions covering financing and site work, together with an analysis establishing when modularization outweighs lost scale economies.
why: It would make firm nuclear capacity deliverable within decarbonization timelines.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2024), [“Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear—Update”](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/LIFTOFF_DOE_Advanced-Nuclear-Update.pdf).

title: Reactor-specific advanced-fuel qualification
open: Can advanced fuels such as TRISO be qualified with defensible bounds on fuel failure and fission-product release under real manufacturing, irradiation, and accident conditions — and can those bounds be transferred validly from small irradiation specimens to full commercial production?
status: Historical TRISO irradiation data provides substantial supporting evidence, and new commercial TRISO-X fuel-fabrication campaigns continued through 2025–2026, with TRISO-X receiving an NRC Special Nuclear Material License for its advanced fuel fabrication facility (U.S. DOE, 2026).
solved_when: Fuel-failure and release bounds are established experimentally for actual manufacturing, irradiation, and accident conditions, and a validated transfer methodology from specimen-scale data to commercial production is demonstrated.
why: Reactor-specific fuel qualification is what allows advanced reactors to be deployed reliably; without application-specific bounds, licensing and operation stall.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2026), [“TRISO-X Receives NRC Special Nuclear Material License for Advanced Fuel Fabrication Facility”](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/triso-x-receives-nrc-special-nuclear-material-license-advanced-fuel-fabrication).

title: Closing a fusion plant’s tritium balance
open: Can a fusion power plant close its tritium fuel cycle — breeding, extracting, processing, and accounting for all retention, losses, and outage effects so that it produces at least as much tritium as it consumes? A demonstration must include the inventories needed for replacement and for starting additional plants.
status: Blanket and tritium extraction concepts exist, but the 2021 National Academies assessment ([NASEM (2021), "Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid"](https://doi.org/10.17226/25991)) identifies integrated closure of the tritium cycle as an outstanding problem.
solved_when: Fuel-cycle self-sufficiency is demonstrated across breeding, extraction, processing, retention, outages, and losses, with tritium inventories sufficient for plant replacement and for outfitting additional plants.
why: Without a closed tritium balance, a fusion fleet cannot sustain itself beyond its initial fuel inventories.
key_works: NASEM (2021), [“Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid”](https://doi.org/10.17226/25991).

title: Fusion components with power-plant availability
open: Can fusion power-plant components be made to survive the combined assault of neutron damage, heat, corrosion, and cyclic stress for economically useful lifetimes, with replacements that are economical too? Formally, the target is integrated lifetime qualification of components under the full simultaneous environment, with remote-maintenance downtime counted against plant availability.
status: Decades of tests have covered parts of the environment individually, but integrated lifetime qualification under the full combined environment remains open. (NASEM (2021), ["Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid"](https://doi.org/10.17226/25991).)
solved_when: Components are demonstrated to endure the combined neutron, thermal, corrosion, and cyclic-stress environment with replacement schedules economical enough — including remote-maintenance downtime — to support power-plant-level availability.
why: Even a successful plasma can yield a failed power plant if components must be replaced so frequently that availability collapses; frequent replacement can erase the value of plasma success.
key_works: NASEM (2021), [“Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid”](https://doi.org/10.17226/25991).

title: Wave-energy control that improves lifetime revenue
open: Can a wave-energy device be designed so that its geometry, power take-off, moorings, and control law are optimized together for total electricity value over the device's lifetime, rather than for short-term energy capture alone? Formally, this asks for a co-design formulation that internalizes fatigue, storm loading, maintenance, and failure costs alongside revenue.
status: Energy-maximizing controllers and co-design methods exist, but robust economic benefits remain incompletely demonstrated. Related efforts include fatigue-aware optimal control and nonlinear hydrodynamic reduction (Ringwood, Zhan and Faedo, 2023, ["Empowering wave energy with control technology: Possibilities and pitfalls"](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.arcontrol.2023.04.004)).
solved_when: A joint optimization of geometry, power take-off, moorings, and control demonstrably improves lifetime electricity value while accounting for fatigue, storms, maintenance, and failure costs, with robust economic benefits shown rather than assumed.
why: Capturing more energy can otherwise cause disproportionate damage to the device, so control strategies that maximize short-term output can destroy lifetime value.
key_works: Ringwood, Zhan and Faedo (2023), [“Empowering wave energy with control technology: Possibilities and pitfalls”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.arcontrol.2023.04.004).

title: Ecological effects of commercial tidal arrays
open: What happens to marine wildlife when single tidal turbines grow into commercial arrays? Specifically, how do collision risk, displacement, and flow modification translate from individual animal responses into population- and food-web-level outcomes?
status: Monitoring at single devices has reduced some uncertainties, but the 2024 OES-Environmental assessment (["State of the Science Report: Environmental Effects of Marine Renewable Energy Development Around the World"](https://tethys.pnnl.gov/publications/state-of-the-science-2024)) still identifies collision risk and array-scale effects as open gaps.
solved_when: Collision, displacement, and food-web effects at array scale are quantified and animal responses plus flow modification are translated into population outcomes.
why: It underpins ecosystem protection and gives regulators an evidence base for permitting commercial tidal arrays.
key_works: OES-Environmental (2024), [“State of the Science Report: Environmental Effects of Marine Renewable Energy Development Around the World”](https://tethys.pnnl.gov/publications/state-of-the-science-2024).

title: Stability certificates for current-limited grid-forming inverters
open: Can we certify that a grid dominated by current-limited grid-forming inverters remains stable through large disturbances? The goal is to derive checkable network-wide stability guarantees that remain valid when current limits, saturation, faults, and energy constraints activate, extending beyond small-perturbation analysis.
status: Droop control and small-signal theory provide the existing foundations; the 2020 NREL roadmap (Lin et al. (2020), "Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters," NREL/TP-5D00-73476) identifies large-disturbance and interaction behavior as unresolved.
solved_when: Checkable stability certificates exist for the network under large disturbances, covering regimes where current limiting, saturation, faults, and energy constraints are active — not only small-signal conditions.
why: Such certificates would establish recovery confidence for renewable-dominated networks, where large-disturbance behavior currently lacks guarantees.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), [“Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters,” NREL/TP-5D00-73476](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy21osti/73476.pdf).

title: Multi-vendor inverter interoperability without proprietary models
open: Can we specify inverter control behavior precisely enough that independently designed, multi-vendor inverters operate stably together — and remain stable through firmware upgrades — without requiring manufacturers to disclose their proprietary control models? In formal terms, the goal is a specification and testing regime under which component-level tests provably predict network-level stability.
status: A 2024 hardware experiment by Wang, Ganguly and Kroposki ([“Performance Evaluation of Multi-Vendor Grid-Forming Inverters for Grid-Connected Operation Through Hardware Experimentation”](https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87199.pdf)) tested three commercial inverters and found problematic operating regimes despite satisfactory performance elsewhere, showing that current practice does not guarantee stable multi-vendor coexistence.
solved_when: A behavioral specification and component-test methodology exists that demonstrably predicts multi-inverter network stability across vendors and firmware versions, validated without unrestricted disclosure of control source or models.
why: It removes the need for bespoke re-integration and restability studies every time a device is added or firmware changes, which currently blocks scalable multi-vendor deployment of grid-forming inverters.
key_works: Wang, Ganguly and Kroposki (2024), [“Performance Evaluation of Multi-Vendor Grid-Forming Inverters for Grid-Connected Operation Through Hardware Experimentation”](https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87199.pdf).

title: Protection with low inverter fault currents
open: Can a power system dominated by inverter-based resources selectively isolate faults when the inverters' current limits erase the fault signatures that conventional protection depends on? A complete answer must establish reliable selectivity under changing network topology, weak communications, and a mix of inverter control schemes.
status: Differential and traveling-wave methods provide partial solutions; coordinated protection remains a roadmap gap, as noted in Lin et al. (2020), ["Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters"](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy21osti/73476.pdf).
solved_when: A protection scheme exists that discriminates and isolates faults selectively — not merely detects them — and whose reliability is demonstrated under changing topology, weak communications, and mixed inverter controls.
why: It prevents faults from triggering unnecessary wide-area disconnections, which would otherwise undermine the reliability of an inverter-dominated grid.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), [“Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters”](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy21osti/73476.pdf).

title: Black start of large inverter-dominated networks
open: Can a large, fully de-energized network dominated by inverters be restored autonomously, coordinating transformer energization, motor starts, load pickup, synchronization, and limited energy availability under uncertain conditions?
status: Microgrid and hardware demonstrations establish feasibility of inverter-driven black start, while 2023–2024 studies — including Baeckeland and Seo (2023), ["Large-Signal Stability Improvement of Parallel Grid-Forming Inverter-Driven Black Start"](https://www.nlr.gov/docs/fy24osti/87250.pdf) — identify saturation and overload instability as key obstacles.
solved_when: A restoration scheme is demonstrated (in simulation or hardware) that black-starts a large inverter-dominated network while stably handling transformer energization, motor starts, load pickup, and synchronization under uncertainty and limited energy budgets.
why: Without a scalable black-start capability, a rare system-wide outage could leave an inverter-dominated grid unable to restore itself, converting a rare event into a prolonged blackout.
key_works: Baeckeland and Seo (2023), [“Large-Signal Stability Improvement of Parallel Grid-Forming Inverter-Driven Black Start”](https://www.nlr.gov/docs/fy24osti/87250.pdf).

title: Resource adequacy under unseen renewable droughts
open: Can a power system with a large share of weather-dependent renewables maintain resource adequacy under rare compound events — joint renewable droughts, heating extremes, hydrological shortages, and equipment failures — that lie outside the historical weather record? Formally, how do we quantify and bound supply-shortfall risk under weather conditions not present in the observational sample, in a changing climate?
status: Multi-year studies have identified vulnerable operating regimes, but extrapolating to rare compound conditions under a changing climate remains unresolved.
solved_when: (as above)
why: An annual energy balance does not guarantee continuous supply; without risk estimates for unseen compound droughts, planners cannot distinguish genuinely reliable systems from ones that merely look adequate on historical data.
key_works: Sundar et al. (2023), [“Meteorological drivers of resource adequacy failures in current and high renewable Western U.S. power systems”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41875-6).

open: Can realistic multiperiod AC dispatch and unit commitment — including discrete decisions and uncertainty — be solved within operational time limits while carrying optimality bounds and credible contingency guarantees?

why: It would extract more service from existing clean generation and transmission, deferring new infrastructure.

title: Selective protection of multi-vendor HVDC meshes
open: How can converters, breakers, and protection functions from different vendors be coordinated in a meshed multiterminal HVDC grid so that a fault is cleared selectively, leaving healthy corridors in service? A satisfactory answer must also keep this coordination interoperable as the grid is expanded or equipment is replaced.
status: Multiterminal HVDC systems and DC breaker demonstrations exist, but the 2021 review by Wang et al. (“Multi-vendor interoperability in HVDC grid protection: State-of-the-art and challenges ahead”) identifies coordination and specification requirements that remain unresolved.
solved_when: A protection coordination scheme exists for multi-vendor HVDC meshes that isolates only faulted corridors while preserving healthy ones, and whose interoperability is maintained through grid expansion and equipment replacement — including a demonstration or specification meeting the coordination and specification requirements the 2021 review identifies as unresolved.
why: Selective, vendor-neutral protection is what makes efficient offshore hubs and long-distance connections to distant renewables operationally viable.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), [“Multi-vendor interoperability in HVDC grid protection: State-of-the-art and challenges ahead”](https://doi.org/10.1049/gtd2.12165).

title: Forecast-aware dynamic transmission ratings
open: Can a transmission network be operated reliably up to weather-dependent dynamic thermal ratings rather than conservative static limits? In particular, can line ratings be computed and used in real time so that sensor error, unobserved hot spans, forecast failure, and rapid wind shifts remain provably bounded, with validated fallback procedures when the forecast fails?
status: Dynamic line ratings are already deployed, and hourly dynamic line rating datasets exist for existing transmission across the contiguous United States (Brown et al. (2024), ["Hourly Dynamic Line Ratings for Existing Transmission Across the Contiguous United States"](https://doi.org/10.2172/2476805)); however, dependable network-wide operational limits remain an engineering challenge.
solved_when: Network-wide operational limits derived from dynamic ratings are shown to be dependable in operation: uncertainty from sensor error, unobserved spans, forecast failure, and rapid wind changes is explicitly bounded, and fallback procedures are validated.
why: Dynamic ratings unlock additional capacity on existing corridors and reduce renewable curtailment without new construction.
key_works: Brown et al. (2024), [“Hourly Dynamic Line Ratings for Existing Transmission Across the Contiguous United States”](https://doi.org/10.2172/2476805).

title: Distribution observability with sparse, asynchronous data
open: Can we reliably estimate the states and topology of a three-phase distribution network from sparse, asynchronous, and delayed sensor data under uncertain equipment models, while protecting the privacy of customers behind those measurements? The goal is an estimator that also outputs calibrated operational uncertainty rather than a single point estimate.
status: Decades of foundational work exist, but the 2023 survey by Yadav et al. (2023), "Review of Emerging Concepts in Distribution System State Estimation: Opportunities and Challenges," identifies sensor limitations, pseudo-measurement dependence, and high-DER penetration as open challenges.
solved_when: A method exists that recovers three-phase states and network topology from sparse, delayed meter data with uncertain equipment, delivers calibrated uncertainty quantification, and preserves privacy — addressing the sensor, pseudo-measurement, and high-DER challenges retained in the 2023 survey.
why: It enables active operation of distribution networks that have historically been operated passively, which is essential as these grids absorb growing distributed energy resources.
key_works: Yadav et al. (2023), [“Review of Emerging Concepts in Distribution System State Estimation: Opportunities and Challenges”](https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3292793).

title: Dependable dynamic hosting capacity
open: How much new generation and flexible demand can a distribution feeder safely host when their output is actively controlled rather than fixed, and when forecasts of both system conditions and customer behavior are uncertain? The question is to characterize the admissible set of connections — ideally with probabilistic guarantees — that remains safe even under communication failures and behavioral changes.
status: Static hosting-capacity maps and pilot demonstrations exist; a 2024 California Energy Commission demonstration ("Electric Access System Enhancement: Assessment of a Distributed Energy Resource Management System for Enabling Dynamic Hosting Capacity") assessed DER coordination but did not settle general probabilistic guarantees.
solved_when: A method exists that determines allowable generation and flexible demand under active control and uncertain forecasts, with guarantees that connections remain safe (no voltage or thermal violations) during communication failures and behavioral changes.
why: It would let utilities expand grid connections and integrate more DERs without voltage or thermal violations, replacing conservative static limits with dependable dynamic capacity.
key_works: California Energy Commission (2024), [“Electric Access System Enhancement: Assessment of a Distributed Energy Resource Management System for Enabling Dynamic Hosting Capacity”](https://www.energy.ca.gov/publications/2024/electric-access-system-enhancement-assessment-distributed-energy-resource).

title: Lean-electrolyte lithium-metal cells under practical conditions
open: Can a lithium-metal cell be built that simultaneously meets all the conditions electric vehicles demand — thin lithium anodes, high-loading cathodes, lean electrolyte, tolerable stack pressure, fast charging, and long cycle life — in a manufacturable large-format cell with realistic safety data?
status: After roughly six decades of research, a 2024 industry assessment (He et al. (2024), ["Industry needs for practical lithium-metal battery designs in electric vehicles"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-024-01624-5)) still records unresolved conflicts among lifetime, gas generation, pressure, and manufacturing.
solved_when: A manufacturable, large-format lithium-metal cell is demonstrated combining thin lithium, high-loading cathodes, minimal liquid electrolyte, tolerable pressure, fast charging, and long life, together with realistic safety data.
why: It is the step that converts high-energy laboratory prototypes into practical batteries for electric vehicles.
key_works: He et al. (2024), [“Industry needs for practical lithium-metal battery designs in electric vehicles”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-024-01624-5).

title: Fast charging across battery age and temperature
open: Can a battery management system reliably detect and avoid lithium plating during rapid charging across cold temperatures, cell aging, and cell-to-cell variation, without excessive heating or sacrificing capacity?
status: Wang et al. (2022) demonstrated 265 Wh/kg cells reaching 70% charge in eleven minutes for over 2,000 cycles under specified conditions.
solved_when: A charging protocol detects and avoids plating under cold, aged, and variable-cell conditions while preserving high specific energy and cycle life; a benchmark is the demonstrated regime of 265 Wh/kg cells reaching 70% charge in eleven minutes for over 2,000 cycles, extended across the stated stressors without added heating or capacity loss.
why: It would make fast charging dependable in real-world conditions and could allow smaller vehicle batteries by removing the need to oversize for charging limitations.
key_works: Wang et al. (2022), [“Fast charging of energy-dense lithium-ion batteries”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05281-0).

title: Solid-state batteries without burdensome stack pressure
open: Can a solid-state battery be engineered to maintain internal contact and suppress filament growth in large-format cells while operating at the modest stack pressures a battery pack can realistically provide, without sacrificing energy density, power, safety, or lifetime?
status: Conductive electrolytes and promising cells exist, but the 2023 assessment by Janek and Zeier, ["Challenges in speeding up solid-state battery development"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-023-01208-9), retains major interfacial and economic obstacles.
solved_when: A large-format cell demonstrates stable contact and filament suppression at pack-compatible stack pressure, with energy, power, safety, and lifetime targets met when the mass and volume of any pressure hardware are included in the accounting.
why: Pressure hardware can consume the anticipated mass and volume benefits of solid-state batteries, eroding the case for adopting them.
key_works: Janek and Zeier (2023), [“Challenges in speeding up solid-state battery development”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-023-01208-9).

title: Cold-climate sodium-ion full cells
open: Can a sodium-ion full cell, built only from scalable materials, keep useful charging behavior, energy, lifetime, and safety in cold climates — and how does it perform at the pack level once the energy needed for heating is counted?
status: Commercial sodium-ion technology provides a base, but a 2024 review (Bai et al., "Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Batteries: Challenges and Progress") shows that transport, interface, and diffusion limitations persist.
solved_when: A full cell made of scalable materials demonstrates retained low-temperature charging, energy, lifetime, and safety, together with pack-level performance that accounts for heating energy.
why: It would give cold regions an affordable storage option that does not depend on scarce or costly materials.
key_works: Bai et al. (2024), [“Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Batteries: Challenges and Progress”](https://doi.org/10.1002/aenm.202303788).

title: Organic flow batteries with economical electrolyte lifetimes
open: Can an aqueous organic flow battery be built whose electrolyte degradation and replacement costs stay economically acceptable over its full service life? Formally, the challenge is to jointly engineer inexpensive active molecules with sufficient stability and solubility, pair them with selective membranes, and enable regeneration, so that no single factor — cost, lifetime, or crossover — undermines the others.
status: A 2023 comparison of 38 materials (Emmel et al., "Benchmarking organic active materials for aqueous redox flow batteries in terms of lifetime and cost," https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42450-9) found only a limited subset economically promising under its assumptions.
solved_when: A complete organic flow battery system is demonstrated in which low-cost active materials, adequate stability and solubility, selective membranes, and electrolyte regeneration are integrated, with degradation and replacement costs remaining acceptable throughout service.
why: Material abundance alone does not ensure lifetime affordability; a solution would make organic flow batteries a viable low-cost, scalable storage technology rather than a laboratory curiosity.
key_works: Emmel et al. (2023), [“Benchmarking organic active materials for aqueous redox flow batteries in terms of lifetime and cost”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42450-9).

title: Reproducible solid-state battery benchmarks
open: How can we design benchmarking protocols and shared datasets for solid-state batteries that predict whether a measurement will reproduce across different laboratories, disentangling the intrinsic contribution of materials from pressure, processing, geometry, and reporting choices? Such a framework should also extend from as-prepared cells to realistic aging conditions.
status: A 2024 round robin study (Puls et al. (2024), ["Benchmarking the reproducibility of all-solid-state battery cell performance"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-024-01634-3)) supplied common materials to 21 groups and documented substantial variability in cell performance.
solved_when: A protocol and publicly available dataset exist that can quantitatively attribute performance variability to materials versus pressure, processing, geometry, and reporting factors, and predict cross-laboratory reproducibility — including under realistic aging.
why: It would make reported results comparable between labs, so that progress in solid-state battery development is measurable rather than noise-dominated, and reduce wasted development effort chasing irreproducible gains.
key_works: Puls et al. (2024), [“Benchmarking the reproducibility of all-solid-state battery cell performance”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-024-01634-3).

why: Affordable multiday storage would let grids ride through renewable droughts with far less fossil-fuel backup capacity.

why: It would cut winter electricity peaks and displace fossil heating by making compact, on-building seasonal heat storage practical where bulky water tanks are not viable.

title: Installed heat-pump performance during cold, humid extremes
open: Can we predict — and then improve — how installed heat pumps hold up in capacity and efficiency when frosting, defrost cycles, and extreme winter demand coincide, including real-world distribution losses and resistive backup operation?

why: It determines winter peak loads and the bills customers actually pay, tying laboratory equipment ratings to real cold, humid extremes.

why: It removes a persistent fossil load in apartment buildings.

title: Low-GWP refrigerants across difficult applications
open: Can high-ambient, large-charge, and retrofit refrigeration systems be served by refrigerants whose lifecycle climate impact is low, without sacrificing flammability, toxicity, pressure, efficiency, and serviceability? Formally, the goal is a refrigerant-and-system design meeting low-GWP lifecycle performance across these difficult application classes while satisfying the full set of safety and performance constraints.
status: Alternatives already solve many applications; the 2024 buildings blueprint (U.S. DOE, "Decarbonizing the U.S. Economy by 2050: A National Blueprint for the Buildings Sector") retains broader availability and deployment as development targets.
solved_when: Low lifecycle climate impact is achieved in high-ambient, large-charge, and retrofit systems while meeting flammability, toxicity, pressure, efficiency, and service requirements.
why: Without such refrigerants, leakage from these hard-to-decarbonize systems erodes the climate gains of electrification.

title: Efficient humidity removal without overcooling
open: Can a building cooling system remove moisture from ventilation air without first chilling that air to its dew point — doing the latent work independently, at low energy and equipment cost? A successful answer would demonstrate durable materials, efficient regeneration, and hygienic operation under realistic ventilation loads.
status: Desiccant systems and separate sensible–latent prototypes already exist; DOE's 2019–2024 program targets the remaining exchanger and integration barriers (U.S. DOE/ORNL, "Separate Sensible and Latent AC System").
solved_when: A separate sensible–latent (SSLC) system is demonstrated that achieves durable materials, efficient regeneration, and hygienic operation under realistic ventilation loads, overcoming the remaining exchanger and integration barriers.
why: Dehumidification can dominate the cooling demand of efficient buildings, so decoupling latent from sensible heat removal directly attacks a leading energy cost.
key_works: U.S. DOE/ORNL (2019–2024), [“Separate Sensible and Latent AC System”](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/separate-sensible-and-latent-ac-system).

title: Durable radiative cooling in humid, dirty cities
open: Can a passive radiative cooling system keep delivering real annual energy savings on an actual building in a humid, polluted city with clouds, soiling, and restricted sky view? More precisely, can such a system be shown to remain effective and maintainable under those conditions while its coupling to the building — including any winter heating penalty — is properly accounted for?
status: Daytime subambient cooling under direct sunlight was first demonstrated in 2014 by Raman et al. (2014), ["Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13883); what remains open is demonstrating durable, climate-specific system value in real urban conditions.
solved_when: A durable, climate-specific system is demonstrated to provide maintainable annual energy savings in a real humid, dirty urban setting (clouds, humidity, pollution, soiling, restricted sky view), with building coupling and winter penalties resolved.
why: A solution would cut cooling electricity demand in cities that need it most and improve urban resilience to heat.
key_works: Raman et al. (2014), [“Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13883).

title: Closing the retrofit prediction–performance gap
open: Can we predict, before a retrofit is installed, how much energy and money it will actually save and how indoor conditions will change, together with calibrated uncertainty on those predictions? More sharply, can we decompose the prediction–performance gap itself, attributing it to installation quality, model error, and behavioral responses across building stocks?
status: The gap between predicted and realized performance has been recognized for decades; the 2018 Weatherization Assistance Program evaluation by Fowlie, Greenstone and Wolfram (2018), ["Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program"](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy005), found major prediction–realization differences in its setting.
solved_when: A method exists that forecasts measured savings, indoor conditions, and costs prior to installation with calibrated uncertainty, and quantifies the separate contributions of installation, model, and behavioral factors to prediction error across building stocks.
why: Reliable ex-ante predictions determine which retrofit projects get selected and financed, and protect households from investing in measures that fail to deliver.
key_works: Fowlie, Greenstone and Wolfram (2018), [“Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program”](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy005).

title: Building controllers that transfer from simulation to deployment
open: Can a building controller trained in simulation preserve its energy and flexibility performance when deployed across unseen buildings, faults, occupants, and weather — without lengthy commissioning? A convincing answer requires testing comfort, safety, and rebound in occupied buildings.
status: Control demonstrations exist, and BOPTEST (Blum et al., 2021, ["Building optimization testing framework (BOPTEST) for simulation-based benchmarking of control strategies in buildings"](https://doi.org/10.1080/19401493.2021.1986574)) introduced standardized simulation-based comparison of control strategies in 2021, but transfer from simulation to deployment remains unresolved.
solved_when: A controller is demonstrated to maintain energy and flexibility benefits in occupied, real buildings under conditions unseen in training (new buildings, faults, occupants, weather), with comfort, safety, and rebound all verified, and without requiring lengthy commissioning.
why: It would make demand-side flexibility from existing building equipment practical rather than confined to simulation.
key_works: Blum et al. (2021), [“Building optimization testing framework (BOPTEST) for simulation-based benchmarking of control strategies in buildings”](https://doi.org/10.1080/19401493.2021.1986574).

title: Passive survivability during compound heat waves and blackouts
open: Which building retrofits can keep indoor conditions within health-based exposure limits during a multiday heat wave when the grid is down and mechanical cooling is unavailable? The question asks for experimentally validated retrofit packages that hold under realistic conditions — vulnerable occupants, humidity, nighttime heat retention, and actual occupant behavior — not just idealized steady-state assumptions.
status: Individual passive measures have been developed, but 2023 compound-event modeling (Stone et al. (2023), ["How Blackouts during Heat Waves Amplify Mortality and Morbidity Risk"](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.2c09588)) showed major risks under compound heat-wave-and-blackout conditions, and building-specific protection thresholds remain unresolved.
solved_when: Retrofit strategies are identified and experimentally validated to maintain health-based exposure limits throughout multiday heat-wave conditions without electricity, accounting for vulnerable occupants, humidity, nighttime heat retention, and realistic occupant behavior.
why: When blackouts coincide with heat waves, occupants relying on mechanical cooling face acute heat exposure; validated passive retrofits would protect them even when cooling systems fail.
key_works: Stone et al. (2023), [“How Blackouts during Heat Waves Amplify Mortality and Morbidity Risk”](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.2c09588).

title: Affordable cooling access without high-emissions lock-in
open: How can underserved households and essential services be provided with reliable, efficient cooling whose running bills remain affordable — and how should actual access, health protection, rebound, leakage, and lifecycle emissions be measured to verify that this is achieved without locking in high emissions?

why: It expands essential protection against heat for vulnerable populations while limiting the climate impacts that conventional cooling scale-up would cause.

title: Reliable megawatt charging for truck corridors
open: Can megawatt-scale charging sites be operated so that freight schedules are served reliably while queues, connector heating, grid demand, and costs stay within acceptable bounds — and can this be validated in practice at busy, multivehicle sites operating across seasons and equipment vendors?
status: Megawatt Charging System tests (e.g., Tolbert et al. (2024), "CharIn Megawatt Charging System: 4th Event Summary Report") provide the technical foundations, but corridor-scale service and grid integration remain deployment challenges.
solved_when: A validated demonstration of corridor-scale megawatt charging at busy multivehicle sites shows reliable service of freight schedules across seasons and vendors, with queueing, connector thermal management, grid demand, and cost all controlled within stated bounds.
why: Long-haul truck electrification depends on trucks being able to charge predictably during their limited mandated breaks; without reliable megawatt charging, corridor-scale freight electrification stalls.

title: Auditable end-to-end public charging reliability
open: How can we measure public charging reliability the way a driver actually experiences it, so that a charger counts as working only when a real user can complete a session end to end — across vehicles, payment systems, accessibility needs, and network coverage? Answering this requires independent, systematically collected datasets of usable service rather than operator-reported uptime.
status: Rempel et al.'s 2022–2024 study tested 657 connectors and documented interoperability, payment, and access failures; their findings appear in "Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers" (Rempel et al., 2024).
solved_when: A definition of end-to-end reliability spanning vehicles, payments, accessibility, and networks is established, together with independently collected datasets measuring usable public charging service.
why: Without auditable end-to-end measurement, reliability statistics can hide failures that strand drivers, and reliable public charging is what makes EV use feasible for the many users who cannot charge at home.

title: Vehicle-to-grid with demonstrated owner compensation

why: Parked vehicles constitute a large pool of flexible capacity that grid services could tap, but only if owners are demonstrably compensated and their batteries and mobility are not sacrificed.

title: Reliable partial electrification of freight rail
open: Can freight trains run reliably on partially electrified lines using battery locomotives alone, with no diesel backup? The challenge is a joint design of locomotive batteries, the placement and length of electrified segments, charging infrastructure, and timetables that together meet payload, lifetime, cost, and reliability requirements under real-world delays and track grades.
status: Electric rail itself is mature; 2024 route simulations (Lu and Allen, 2024, "Intermittent Electrification with Battery Locomotives and the Post-Diesel Future of North American Freight Railroads") support the feasibility of intermittent electrification, but complete operational evidence remains limited.
solved_when: A validated joint design methodology exists for which route simulations demonstrate that battery locomotives sustain rated payloads and schedules over demanding grades and delay scenarios, while meeting battery lifetime and cost targets without diesel backup.
why: It unlocks electrification of freight corridors where continuous overhead catenary is impractical or too expensive, removing diesel dependence on such routes.

title: Mission-qualified high-specific-energy aircraft batteries
open: Can a battery pack be built that meets the full set of demands an electric aircraft mission places on it at once — enough specific energy for the mission, power at takeoff, energy reserves, crash safety, thermal control, and economical cycling? Formally, the goal is a pack-level design satisfying all of these constraints simultaneously rather than excelling on any single metric.
status: NASA reported 500 Wh/kg SABERS demonstrations in 2022 [NASA (2022), "Solid-state Architecture Batteries for Enhanced Rechargeability and Safety (SABERS) for Electric Aircraft"; Gould and Fitzgerald (2022), "NASA's Solid-State Battery Research Exceeds Initial Goals, Draws Interest"], but this did not establish a mission-qualified large-aircraft pack.
solved_when: A pack-level battery demonstrates mission energy, takeoff power, reserves, crash safety, thermal control, and economical cycling simultaneously, qualifying it for a large-aircraft mission.
why: Aviation's mass, power, and safety constraints are uniquely punishing, so a pack that clears all of them at once is the gateway to electrified flight; progress on any single constraint alone does not deliver that.
key_works: NASA (2022), [“Solid-state Architecture Batteries for Enhanced Rechargeability and Safety (SABERS) for Electric Aircraft”](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220012921); Gould and Fitzgerald (2022), [“NASA’s Solid-State Battery Research Exceeds Initial Goals, Draws Interest”](https://www.nasa.gov/aeronautics/nasas-solid-state-battery-research-exceeds-initial-goals-draws-interest/).

title: Flight-qualified megawatt aircraft circuit protection
open: Can a megawatt-class aircraft circuit protection system be qualified to survive lifetime electrical and thermal stresses while reliably detecting DC arcs and isolating faults in coordination with the rest of the powertrain — including validating insulation performance against high-altitude service degradation?

why: The mass and losses of the protection system directly determine whether megawatt electric propulsion is viable on aircraft; heavy or inefficient protection erodes the benefit of electrification.

title: Ammonia engines with low nitrous oxide and ammonia slip
open: Can an ammonia-fueled marine engine run efficiently through transient and low-load duty cycles while keeping N₂O, ammonia slip, and NOₓ emissions low — and can that performance be validated in fleet duty, including aftertreatment behavior and engine aging?
status: Zhou et al. (2024) improved modeled/design performance using reforming and recirculation in "Ammonia marine engine design for enhanced efficiency and reduced greenhouse gas gas emissions" (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46452-z), but fleet-duty validation remains open.
solved_when: An ammonia marine engine demonstrates efficient operation across transient and low-load duties with suppressed N₂O, NH₃ slip, and NOₓ, and this performance — including aftertreatment and engine aging — is validated under fleet-duty conditions rather than only in modeled or design studies.
why: Nitrogen emissions (N₂O, NH₃ slip, NOₓ) can undermine the low-carbon benefit of ammonia as a marine fuel, so without demonstrated suppression in real duty cycles the climate case for ammonia propulsion collapses.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2024), [“Ammonia marine engine design for enhanced efficiency and reduced greenhouse gas emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46452-z).

title: Bankable fuel savings from wind-assisted shipping
open: Can the annual fuel savings delivered by wind-assisted propulsion systems be verified independently and predictably across real-world variation in routes, vessels, weather, and loading conditions — and can propulsion and routing be optimized in a way that accounts for maintenance, stability, deck-space use, and scheduling constraints?
status: Commercial installations demonstrate savings, but the evidence base remains application-specific; Lloyd's Register's 2024 research on applying wind-assisted propulsion to ships retains open integration and evidence gaps.
solved_when: Verified, route- and vessel-specific annual savings figures exist across the range of operating weather and loading conditions, together with an optimization framework for propulsion and routing that integrates maintenance, stability, deck use, and scheduling.
why: Reliable, bankable savings estimates would let shipowners finance retrofits of existing vessels with confidence, directly cutting fuel demand from the current fleet rather than waiting for new builds.
key_works: Lloyd’s Register (2024), [“Applying wind-assisted propulsion to ships”](https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/research-reports/2024/applying-wind-assisted-propulsion-to-ships/).

title: Minigrid viability with uncertain productive demand
open: How can a minigrid be financed so that it remains reliable and affordable when future demand and household income growth are deeply uncertain? In particular, which combinations of appliance finance, tariff design, productive-use promotion, and arrangements for eventual main-grid arrival make projects bankable under that uncertainty?
status: Successful systems already exist, and ESMAP's 2022 handbook ("Mini Grids for Half a Billion People: Market Outlook and Handbook for Decision Makers") identifies demand, finance, and portfolio scaling as the key barriers.
solved_when: A validated framework (or implemented financing arrangement) demonstrates that minigrids can be financed reliably and affordably despite uncertain demand and income growth, with appliance finance, tariffs, productive uses, and main-grid-arrival arrangements each empirically validated as part of the viable mix.
why: Without a workable model, minigrids risk collapse once initial grants end and commissioning support dries up; a solution sustains electricity access over the long term.

title: Sustained displacement of polluting cooking by electricity
open: Can electric cooking technologies be designed and deployed so that households actually abandon polluting fuels for years rather than merely adding a new stove alongside them? solved_when: Electric cooking solutions demonstrably displace polluting fuels over multi-year horizons across these constraints, with measured reductions in stove stacking and household pollution exposure.
why: It ties decarbonization directly to household health outcomes and time savings, making climate action deliver immediate, measurable benefits to affected families.

title: Retrofitting continuous furnaces above 1,000°C
open: Can a continuously operated furnace running above 1,000°C be retrofitted from combustion to electric heating while preserving throughput, product atmosphere and quality, and refractory life, all under constrained electrical connections? A successful design must match the incumbent furnace on each of these process-critical dimensions, not merely deliver the required heat.
status: Electric furnaces already serve selected industrial processes, but the U.S. DOE's 2022 Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap identifies cross-sector retrofit barriers — of which constrained electrical connections are one — as an obstacle to broader adoption.
solved_when: A retrofit design for a continuous furnace operating above 1,000°C is demonstrated to maintain throughput, atmosphere control, product quality, and refractory lifetime at parity with the combustion baseline, within the limits of the site's available electrical connections.
why: It decarbonizes high-temperature industrial heat without waiting for entire plants to be rebuilt, turning furnace replacement from a site-level capital event into a component-level retrofit.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2022), [“Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap”](https://www.energy.gov/eere/doe-industrial-decarbonization-roadmap).

title: Electrochemical lime without displaced emissions

solved_when: A scaled process demonstrates closed-loop reagent recycling producing cement-compatible calcium feedstock at lower total emissions and cost than conventional lime production, with all energy inputs (electricity) and separated-carbon handling accounted for in the total.
why: Cement's process emissions come from decomposing limestone itself, so they persist even if furnace heat is fully electrified; solving this closes the remaining emission source in lime production.
key_works: Leão et al. (2024), [“ZeroCAL: Eliminating Carbon Dioxide Emissions from Limestone’s Decomposition to Decarbonize Cement Production”](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.4c03193).

solved_when: A process recovers paste from actual mixed demolition waste and converts it into consistent clinker, with separation energy and contamination (of steelmaking) kept within acceptable bounds, at a scale compatible with furnace capacity despite feedstock variability.
why: It reuses calcium that has already been decarbonated, avoiding the CO₂ released when virgin limestone is calcined.

open: Can we predict, decades in advance, when reinforcement corrosion will initiate in concretes made with new low-clinker binders — under the coupled action of carbonation, chlorides, cracking, and humidity? why: Without trustworthy long-term predictions, structures may be replaced prematurely, erasing the emissions savings that motivate low-clinker concrete in the first place.

title: Hydrogen reduction of variable iron ores
open: Can we predict — and then suppress — sticking, pore closure, and sluggish final-stage reduction when hydrogen is used to reduce iron ores whose gangue composition and pellet microstructure vary from feedstock to feedstock? In other words, is there a quantitative model linking ore variability to reduction behavior that also tells us how to prevent these degradation modes?
status: Selected reduction configurations are established, but Raabe's 2023 synthesis (["The Materials Science behind Sustainable Metals and Alloys"](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.2c00799)) documents that the coupling between reduction kinetics, evolving microstructure, and feedstock variability remains unresolved.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework accounts for the effects of variable gangue and pellet microstructure on sticking, pore closure, and final-stage reduction kinetics, and identifies operating or design conditions that suppress these failure modes across realistic feedstock variability.
why: It would free hydrogen-based direct reduction from dependence on premium, narrow-specification ores, broadening the feedstock base for fossil-free steelmaking.

why: Success would replace carbon reductants with electricity in primary ironmaking, eliminating the process's CO₂ emissions at the smelting step.

title: Low-iridium PEM electrolysis with long life
open: Can proton-exchange-membrane water electrolyzers run at industrial current densities and multiyear stack lifetimes using far less iridium than today's standard? solved_when: An electrolyzer stack operates at industrial current density with greatly reduced iridium loading, preserving gas purity and multiyear lifetime under realistic power cycling.
why: Iridium scarcity threatens to cap the scale-up of green hydrogen production; solving it removes a hard supply bottleneck on electrolyzer deployment.

why: It would cut both catalyst and balance-of-plant costs for hydrogen production by removing the need for corrosive concentrated alkaline handling.

why: It determines how feasibly fertilizer, iron, and fuels production can switch to clean hydrogen at industrial scale.

title: Hydrogen leakage and atmospheric feedbacks
open: How much hydrogen actually leaks across the supply chain, and how much do those leaks perturb the atmosphere through changes in methane lifetime, ozone, and stratospheric water vapor — given that the dominant sink, soil uptake, is itself poorly quantified?
status: The state of the art is a 2023 multimodel assessment (Sand et al. 2023, "A multi-model assessment of the Global Warming Potential of hydrogen") estimating the 100-year warming potential near 12 with substantial uncertainty; actual leakage rates remain incompletely observed.
solved_when: Leakage rates along the hydrogen supply chain are directly measured rather than inferred, and the resulting perturbations to methane lifetime, ozone, and stratospheric water vapor are constrained well enough to pin down hydrogen's 100-year warming potential within a tight range rather than the broad uncertainty band around the current estimate of roughly 12.
why: Without these observations, the claimed climate benefit of switching to hydrogen could be materially overstated or understated, since leakage-driven methane increases can offset much of the CO2 avoided.
key_works: Sand et al. (2023), [“A multi-model assessment of the Global Warming Potential of hydrogen”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-023-00857-8).

why: It determines whether existing hydrogen infrastructure can be safely reused or must be replaced, directly governing the cost and timeline of hydrogen pipeline deployment.

title: Predictive social tipping rather than retrospective narratives
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Can we identify measurable conditions under which changes in social norms, institutions, investments, or technology adoption become self-sustaining — and can interventions designed from those conditions be tested prospectively across different settings?
status: Otto et al. (2020) identify candidate social tipping processes for stabilizing Earth's climate by 2050, but calibrated thresholds and success probabilities remain unavailable.
solved_when: Calibrated thresholds for self-sustaining social tipping are established, together with forward-looking tests of interventions (with success probabilities) carried out across multiple settings, rather than retrospective case narratives.
why: It would reveal effective, testable ways to accelerate collective change toward climate stabilization, replacing after-the-fact storytelling with predictive leverage.
key_works: Otto et al. (2020), [“Social tipping dynamics for stabilizing Earth’s climate by 2050”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1900577117).

title: Fossil phaseout without an extraction race
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: How can policy credibly phase out fossil fuels while leaving resources in the ground, without triggering an anticipatory race to extract or shifting losses onto particular owners and groups? Formally, the task is to design a phaseout-and-compensation mechanism that limits anticipatory extraction, ownership transfers made to escape liability, and the disproportionate concentration of burdens.
status: Green-paradox theory is longstanding, and Semieniuk et al. (2022), ["Stranded fossil-fuel assets translate to major losses for investors in advanced economies"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-022-01356-y), clarify who bears ownership exposure to stranding — but the underlying policy incentives remain unresolved.
solved_when: A mechanism (theoretical construction and analysis) exists that credibly deters or bounds anticipatory extraction, prevents avoidance via ownership transfers, and distributes burdens without disproportionate incidence, while ensuring resources remain unextracted.
why: It would connect financial restructuring of fossil-fuel assets directly to lower cumulative extraction, turning stranded-asset risk into a workable policy lever rather than a source of green-paradox escalation.
key_works: Semieniuk et al. (2022), [“Stranded fossil-fuel assets translate to major losses for investors in advanced economies”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-022-01356-y).

title: Reconciling product, corporate, and national carbon accounts
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Can product-level process data, corporate inventories, and national input–output accounts be joined into a single coherent system in which territorial, consumption, and corporate carbon figures reconcile — with every flow accounted for exactly once? Formally, the goal is a unified data architecture whose aggregation and boundary definitions align these three accounting perspectives without hidden omissions or double counting.
status: EXIOBASE (Stadler et al. 2018, ["EXIOBASE 3: Developing a Time Series of Detailed Environmentally Extended Multi-Regional Input-Output Tables"](https://doi.org/10.1111/jiec.12715)) provides substantial coverage, but aggregation choices, boundary mismatches, and missing primary data prevent exact reconciliation.
solved_when: Territorial, consumption, and corporate inventories derived from the joined system reconcile exactly, with no hidden omissions or double counting across the product, corporate, and national levels.
why: It would make responsibility attributions and policy-effect estimates directly comparable across scales, which fragmented accounts currently cannot support.
key_works: Stadler et al. (2018), [“EXIOBASE 3: Developing a Time Series of Detailed Environmentally Extended Multi-Regional Input-Output Tables”](https://doi.org/10.1111/jiec.12715).

title: Tenfold-cheaper auditable product-footprint data
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Can we make an independently auditable product lifecycle-inventory dataset an order of magnitude cheaper to produce than a specified manual baseline — without giving up coverage, calibrated uncertainty, confidentiality, or reproducibility?
status: Databases such as ecoinvent supply essential infrastructure for lifecycle-inventory data (Wernet et al. 2016, "The ecoinvent database version 3 (part I): overview and methodology," https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-016-1087-8), but this tenfold cost-reduction target is formulated here and has no standardized field record.
solved_when: A demonstrated workflow cuts auditable lifecycle-inventory production cost by tenfold relative to the specified manual baseline while preserving coverage, calibrated uncertainty, confidentiality, and reproducibility.
why: It would make product-specific procurement and supply-chain decisions affordable at scale.
key_works: Wernet et al. (2016), [“The ecoinvent database version 3 (part I): overview and methodology”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-016-1087-8).
